10580-the-positive-school-of-criminology:
Italian criminologist Enrico Ferri gave these three lectures at the University of Naples on April 22, 23, and 24, 1901, and Ernest Untermann's translation appeared in Chicago in 1908. Ferri speaks for the "positive" school of criminology, which studied crime as a fact of nature and society rather than as a free choice of the will alone.

The lectures argue that crime grows from a mix of personal traits, social conditions, and circumstance, and that punishment should fit the danger a person poses, not just the act done. Ferri urges prevention, reform, and scientific study over harsh revenge. Readers get a short, forceful statement of ideas that reshaped how courts and reformers thought about crime.
10665-life-letters-and-epicurean-philoso:
Ninon de l'Enclos, the celebrated beauty and wit of seventeenth-century Paris, is the subject of this 1903 volume of life, letters, and philosophy. Chapters follow her youth, her mother's death, her growing fame, her friendships, and her lovers, including the Villarceaux affair and the Marquis de Sevigne. Her letters to Sevigne and her exchange with Saint-Evremond are printed in full.

The book presents Ninon as a free mind who lived by pleasure, reason, and loyalty to friends, in the manner of Epicurus. It also paints the morals and manners of her age. Readers get a vivid portrait of a woman who defied convention and stayed famous into a remarkable old age.
10726-outlines-of-lessons-in-botany-part:
Jane H. Newell wrote Outlines of Lessons in Botany, Part I, From Seed to Leaf, in 1888 for teachers and for mothers studying with their children. Illustrated by H. P. Symmes, the book begins with plants and their uses for food, clothing, air, and fuel. It then guides young learners to raise seedlings in the schoolroom.

Lessons study morning-glory, sunflower, bean, and pea, compare roots such as carrot, onion, and potato, and examine buds of horsechestnut, magnolia, and lilac. Directions are practical and clear. Families and schools get a gentle, hands-on botany course, built on watching real plants grow.
11077-ebooks-neither-e-nor-books-paper-f:
Cory Doctorow delivered this paper at the O'Reilly Emerging Technologies Conference in San Diego on February 12, 2004, under the title Ebooks: Neither E, Nor Books. Doctorow had released two novels and most of a story collection online under a Creative Commons licence. He argues that ebooks then were neither good electronic texts nor good books.

Doctorow discusses piracy panic, writers using false names on ebook newsgroups for fear of retaliation, and mischievous book-rippers said to plant deliberate errors, a claim he doubts for lack of evidence. The talk, dedicated to the public domain, captures early ebook debates: access, copying, and authors' fears, before ereaders and phones changed the market.
11397-the-works-of-samuel-johnson-ll-d-i:
Volume three of Samuel Johnson's Works, in the 1825 nine-volume edition, contains the second volume of the Rambler, essays numbered 106 through 135 and beyond. Topics include the vanity of authors' expectations, Properantia's hopes of confusion, the misery of prostitutes, life well employed, the education of a fop. repentance, youth's haste, Hymenæus's courtship, punishments proportioned to crimes, the young trader turned gentleman, the narrowness of fame, and the dangers of imitating Spenser.

Johnson's Rambler essays, published twice weekly in the 1750s, made his reputation as a moralist. This volume shows his range: character sketches, literary criticism, and moral argument in balanced prose. Readers approaching Johnson will find the Rambler here in a standard collected form.
1149-from-london-to-land-s-end-and-two-l:
Daniel Defoe, author of Robinson Crusoe, rides from London to Land's End and writes what he sees. His subjects are towns, ports, mines, and markets, with notes on trade, roads, and the people who work them. The journey runs through the West Country in the early eighteenth century.

Defoe's eye is that of a merchant and a journalist: he counts ships, weighs wool, and judges inns. The letters add gossip and detail from the road. The book gives a lively, ground-level view of Georgian England, and it still serves historians and travelers alike.
11771-occasional-papers-selected-from-th:
R. W. Church's Occasional Papers, second volume, gathers pieces from the Guardian, the Times, and the Saturday Review between 1846 and 1890. Church, sometime rector of Whatley and Dean of St. Paul's, writes first on Gladstone and the royal supremacy, Joyce on spiritual courts, and Privy Council judgments.

Later papers take up the Purchas case, disendowment, Mozley's Bampton lectures, and Renan's Vie de Jésus, Les Apôtres, and Souvenirs d'enfance. Lives of Frederick Robertson, Baron Bunsen, and Bishop Wilberforce close the set. The volume is a churchman's criticism of his age, collected after his death.
12006-a-handbook-to-agra-and-the-taj-sik:
E. B. Havell's 1904 Handbook to Agra and the Taj, Sikandra, Fatehpur-Sikri, and the Neighbourhood guides visitors through Mughal India, opening with a historical introduction on the great Moguls. Chapters trace Babar's connection with Agra, Humayun and the interregnum of Sher Shah, Akbar, Jahangir, Shah Jahan and his monuments, and Aurangzib.

Havell, an art historian, pairs history with description, so a traveller can move from the story of a ruler to the building he left behind. The handbook covers the Taj itself, Sikandra, and Fatehpur-Sikri, treating architecture as the record of a dynasty. It remains useful as a compact, scholarly companion to one of India's most visited regions.
12045-women-in-the-fine-arts-from-the-se:
Clara Erskine Clement's 1904 book Women in the Fine Arts, from the seventh century B.C. to the twentieth century A.D., opens with an Alinari photograph of Elisabetta Sirani's Infant Christ in the Bologna Gallery. Clement's prefatory note explains that she sent a circular to many artists in Great Britain, Europe, and the United States, asking where their work could be studied.

The book surveys women painters, sculptors, and illustrators across more than two thousand years, from ancient Greece to modern studios. Clement's survey was pioneering: it treated women artists as a continuous tradition, not as exceptions. It remains a useful guide to names and works that larger histories had overlooked.
12050-the-works-of-samuel-johnson-ll-d-i:
Volume 4 of Samuel Johnson's works, printed in 1825 as part of the nine-volume Oxford edition, gathers The Adventurer and The Idler. Its prefatory notice explains that The Adventurer was projected in 1752 by Dr. John Hawkesworth, partly from admiration of The Rambler, which had then ceased to appear.

Hawkesworth's style and sentiments, the notice says, evidently followed Johnson's example from the start, and Johnson himself contributed to the periodical. The volume preserves two of the great eighteenth-century essay series, in which short, moral. Literary pieces addressed readers week by week on manners, books, and human nature.
12455-legends-of-the-middle-ages-narrate:
H. A. Guerber's 1896 retelling gathers the legends that fed medieval literature and art, written to familiarise young students with them. Charlemagne and Roland, King Arthur, Tristan and Isolde, and other heroes of romance appear in plain narrative, each tale chosen for its place in later books, pictures and music.

Guerber links story to source, showing how a legend lived on in poetry, drama and painting after its first telling. The preface frames the book as a doorway, not a scholarly study: enough plot, character and wonder to let a reader meet the old tales and then follow them further. Its value lies in that map-making, joining many separate cycles into one readable whole.
12523-crusaders-of-new-france-a-chronicl:
William Bennett Munro's 1918 chronicle, in the Chronicles of America series, tells of crusaders of New France, the fleur-de-lis in the wilderness. Dedicated to Father Henri Beaudé, the book moves from France of the Bourbons and a voyageur of Brittany to the founding of New France. The age of Louis Quatorze and the iron governor follow.

La Salle and the voyageurs, the church, seigneurs, coureurs-de-bois, agriculture, industry, trade and daily life follow. Munro writes a clear, popular history of French Canada, fond of its missionaries, soldiers and traders. The volume offers a compact, readable account of a French empire in America, and of the people who carried its flag inland.
12807-dick-prescott-s-fourth-year-at-wes:
Dick Prescott's fourth year at West Point, in Hancock's companion volume to the Annapolis finale, moves toward shoulder straps. Dick reports a brother cadet, faces Jordan's revenge, and endures the cadet silence, a cold shoulder from his class. A class meeting, a baseball gait found late, and the Army-Navy game build to the close.

A quiet study scene, where Dick finds a report he should have turned in before supper formation, shows academy routine pressing on honour. Greg Holmes stands by through each trial. The book gives Dick's West Point years their graduation payoff, with sport, loyalty, and duty in balance.
13133-ten-reasons-proposed-to-his-advers:
Edmund Campion, a Jesuit priest, wrote his Ten Reasons in Latin as a challenge to dispute in the Oxford divinity schools. This edition gives the Latin text with an English translation, plus a preface on the work's long fame. Campion's tract passed through forty-seven editions across Europe, and the humanist Muret called it written by the finger of God.

The translator calls it no dry divinity, but a knight's trumpet call to come forth and argue. Its ten theses defend the Catholic faith against all comers, with citations from fathers and councils in the notes. The book is a landmark of Reformation debate, valued for its bold form as much as for its arguments.
1323-history-of-the-conquest-of-peru-wit:
William Hickling Prescott opens this history with a full view of Inca civilization: its roads, laws, religion, and arts, before Pizarro's ships appear. The narrative then follows the conquest itself, from Cajamarca's ambush to the wars among the Spaniards who divided the spoil.

Prescott's preliminary chapters give the Incas their due as builders and rulers, not mere victims, while his tale of the conquest keeps a novelist's pace. The history, a companion to his Mexico, remains a landmark of American scholarship. It draws readers who want the whole Peruvian story.
13614-studies-in-the-psychology-of-sex-v:
The fifth volume of Havelock Ellis's Studies in the Psychology of Sex, published in 1927, takes up erotic symbolism, the mechanism of detumescence, and the psychic state in pregnancy. Ellis groups under symbolism a wide range of sexual variations, arguing that they share a common root in the way desire fastens on images, objects, and acts.

Case notes, medical reports, and historical examples fill the pages, from fetishism to the dreams and delusions of patients in asylums. The closing study turns to pregnancy, tracing changes of mood and mind in expectant mothers. Ellis writes with the same cool, systematic manner as in earlier volumes, aiming to replace moral judgment with description and explanation.
13750-the-heavenly-footman-or-a-descript:
John Bunyan wrote The Heavenly Footman as a short guide to earnest Christian life. The title pictures the believer as a runner in a race, urged to run so as to obtain the prize. Bunyan opens with an epistle to slothful and careless people. He warns that desire alone kills the slothful, and that wasted time shames the soul.

Chapters compare earthly racing with the race for heaven. Runners must press on, not merely start well. Bunyan uses plain images from sport, harvest, and daily work. The style is direct and urgent, in the manner of Pilgrim's Progress. The tract suits readers of Puritan devotion and Bunyan's plain theology.
13941-the-divine-right-of-church-governm:
Sundry ministers of Christ within London wrote this treatise on the divine right of Presbyterian church government. A new, corrected edition argues that preaching and ruling elders, in sessional, presbyterial, and synodical assemblies, hold the only lawful divine claim. Scripture, the authors hold, warrants that order alone. An appendix adds extracts on church membership and ministry.

The appendix treats scriptural qualifications of members, ministers' sole right to preach, and the people's right to choose pastors. Earlier writers had vindicated parts of church government, but none, the authors claim, had laid open divine right as a system. The book belongs to seventeenth-century Presbyterian polemic. It suits students of church polity and Puritan thought.
13958-the-authoritative-life-of-general-:
G. S. Railton, first commissioner to General Booth, wrote this authoritative life of the Salvation Army's founder. William Booth, born April 10, 1829, died August 20, 1912. Chapters follow childhood poverty, salvation in youth, lay ministry, and early ministry. Fight against formality, revivalism, and the East London beginning follow.

Later chapters cover army-making, army leading, desperate fighting, and growth in America and Australasia. Railton, with a preface by Bramwell Booth, writes as an insider. He shows Booth building a disciplined, uniformed Christian mission. The book suits readers of religious and social history. It remains the standard early life of Booth.
14590-a-new-hochelagan-burying-ground-di:
W. D. Lighthall's 1898 privately printed notes report a newly found Hochelagan burying ground at Westmount, on the western spur of Mount Royal in Montreal, discovered between July and September 1898. The title calls itself provisional on the term Hochelagan.

The ground, probably of the people of old Hochelaga or their Mohawk kin, held powerful men in their prime and one young woman. Large stones lay above the bodies, and flat stones had served as scoops. The plateau, sheltered and sunny, suited corn and beans. The notes are a careful early record of Montreal archaeology.
14902-deadwood-dick-the-prince-of-the-ro:
Edward L. Wheeler's 1877 dime novel, number one in Beadle's Half Dime Library, introduces Deadwood Dick, prince of the road and black rider of the Black Hills. Fearless Frank comes to the rescue as the story opens on the plains midway between Cheyenne and the Black Hills.

A wagon train has halted for a noonday feed, not a railway train but white-covered prairie schooners drawn by strong mules, drawn in a circle about a campfire roasting venison. Rough, bearded men gather round, with one exception. Wheeler writes western adventure at full gallop: outlaws, rescues and a masked rider who would run through many sequels.
15126-lecture-on-the-aborigines-of-newfo:
Joseph Noad, surveyor-general of Newfoundland, gave this lecture at St. John's Mechanics' Institute in January 1859, and it was printed there the same year. He opens with rival theories of where North America's native peoples came from, weighing Tatar, lost-tribe, and northeast Asian origins. The Asian route, he notes, was the view most often held.

Noad then turns to Newfoundland's own native people, the Beothuk, and to what was known of their life and fate. His tone is that of a colonial official speaking to a learned local crowd. Read today, the lecture is both a source on Beothuk history and a record of Victorian ideas about race and origins.
15171-journals-of-travels-in-assam-burma:
William Griffith's journals, arranged by John McClelland from an 1847 edition, record travels in Assam, Burma, Bhutan, Afghanistan, and nearby lands. Chapters follow an Assam deputation to examine the tea plant, a Mishmee mountain excursion, and journeys from Upper Assam toward Ava and Rangoon. Plant notes fill many pages.

Griffith, a botanist, writes with a naturalist's eye for tea sites, river routes, and plant distribution, alongside travel hardship. A Linnaean Society notice fronts the book. Scholars of botany, empire, and Asian travel will find the journals detailed, rugged, and rich in firsthand observation.
15188-the-outdoor-chums-after-big-game-o:
Captain Quincy Allen's 1911 Outdoor Chums book sends the Rod, Gun and Camera Club after big game in the wilderness. A frontispiece shows a beast galloping in mad rage straight toward the boys. Chapters open with glorious news, motorcycle thieves, and a moonlit ride home, then start Hank right and head west.

Perilous adventures follow: hunts, camps, and narrow escapes, told in the brisk series style for boys. The chums use pluck, friendship, and outdoor skill to pull through. Young readers who like hunting tales and camp stories will enjoy the book's pace, even where its views of game now feel dated.
15401-the-great-lone-land-a-narrative-of:
Colonel W. F. Butler published this narrative of travel in the North-West of America in 1872, with a route map. The preface opens at York Factory on Hudson Bay, with a man resolved to write a book of all he had seen, and all he had not seen. Butler then tells his own journey west, in a land of rivers, plains, and distant settlements.

Chapters cross the Atlantic, pass through Boston, New York, Niagara, and Quebec, and push on to the Red River country. There Butler meets the half-breeds, the early settlers, and Louis Riel, and recounts the Red River revolt and the murder of Scott. The book blends adventure, report, and reflection on a frontier changing hands. It remains a vivid firsthand account of the Canadian West just as it opened to new rule.
15599-the-collected-works-of-ambrose-bie:
This eighth volume of the collected works of Ambrose Bierce first appeared in 1911. Gordian Press reprinted it in New York in 1966. It gathers negligible tales, On with the Dance, and epigrams. The contents divide into tale groups: negligible tales, the parenticide club, the fourth estate, and the ocean wave, followed by a review section.

Negligible tales include a bottomless grave, Jupiter Doke brigadier-general, the widower Turmore, and the city of the gone away. The parenticide club offers my favorite murder, oil of dog, and the hypnotist. The fourth estate satirizes journalists and the press, while the ocean wave gives shipwreck tales and a captain of the Camel. On with the Dance reviews letters and life with Bierce's bite. The volume shows his dark wit at full stretch: irony, horror, and satire in short, sharp form.
15694-a-friend-of-c-sar-a-tale-of-the-fa:
William Stearns Davis published this tale of the fall of the Roman Republic, set in 50 to 47 B.C., in New York in 1900, with Grosset and Dunlap. An epigraph from Vergil reminds Romans that theirs is the art of ruling peoples, sparing the weak, and flinging the haughty from high seats. Davis dedicates the book to his father, William Vail Wilson Davis, who taught him more than all his books.

Contents run from Praeneste and the upper walks of society through the privilege of a vestal, Pompeius Magnus, and Agias's adventure to the great proconsul and the new consuls. The seventh of January, the Rubicon, and the profitable career of Gabinius follow. Cleopatra enters late. Davis writes a historical novel of Caesar's rise and the Republic's fall, seen through a friend's eyes, with politics, war, and love in the last years of Rome.
1576-a-unique-story-of-a-marvellous-care:
Joel Benton tells the life of Phineas T. Barnum, the showman who built the American museum, the circus, and a career of marvels. Barnum's freak shows, hoaxes, and promotions made him famous on two continents. Barnum, born in 1810, built his American Museum in New York in the 1840s.

Benton follows Barnum from Connecticut shopkeeping to great wealth, politics, and philanthropy, stressing his energy and humour. The life gives a lively portrait of a man who turned wonder into business. His circus, later joined with Bailey's, became the Greatest Show on Earth.
15911-narrative-of-a-voyage-to-the-north:
A personal narrative by Gabriel Franchere of a voyage to the Northwest Coast in 1811 to 1814, or the first American settlement on the Pacific. J. V. Huntington translated and edited the work, issued by Redfield in New York in 1854. An illustration shows Astoria as it was in 1813. Franchere writes as a witness, with spelling and style kept as in his own hand.

Franchere sailed with the Astor expedition to found a fur post at the Columbia's mouth. Hardships, native peoples, and rival traders fill his account. Astoria's rise and fall unfold through daily detail. The narrative stands as a firsthand record of America's Pacific beginning: brave, rough, and far from home.
15966-a-voyage-of-consolation-being-in-t:
A travel novel by Sara Jeannette Duncan, writing as Mrs. Everard Cotes, in a uniform edition with her other books. A Voyage of Consolation follows A Social Departure, in which Orthodocia and her friend went round the world by themselves. Duncan, a Canadian wit, writes of travel with humour and sharp eyes. The book was issued in cloth at one dollar and fifty cents.

The voyage offers consolation after sorrow, with new lands, new friends, and old jokes renewed. Duncan's heroines talk, observe, and laugh their way across seas. The tone stays bright and companionable. The novel delights as a sequel for readers who loved the first voyage: the same brave girls, a wider world, and comfort found in going on.
16017-the-poor-scholar-traits-and-storie:
William Carleton's tale opens in bitter November weather on a barren Irish hill called Esker Dhu. Dominick M'Evoy and his son Jemmy dig potatoes in thin clothes while sleet drives across the slope. The old man, worn by years of rack-rent farming on poor soil, can barely keep at his toil. The son bears the cold better, but both must turn their sides to each storm gust.

From that hard farm life grows the story of a poor scholar, a young man whose learning sets him apart from the labor around him. Carleton writes with sympathy for Irish cottagers and anger at the rents that grind them down. The tale offers a vivid, human picture of poverty, schooling, and family duty in rural Ireland.
16276-the-power-of-faith-exemplified-in-:
This new edition of The Power of Faith tells the life and writings of Mrs. Isabella Graham, enriched by her narrative of her husband's death and other letters. Entered in 1843 by Joanna Bethune and published by the American Tract Society in New York and Boston, the book opens with Graham's early life and residence in Canada. Birth, schooling, conversion, marriage, and a voyage to Quebec lay the foundation of her character.

Later chapters follow her widowhood, charity, and faith in action, with Proverbs on humility and the widow's border as its text. Graham became a model of evangelical benevolence in early America. Readers of religious biography will find an earnest, moving portrait of piety put to work.
17075-dialogue-of-comfort-against-tribul:
St. Thomas More's Dialogue of Comfort Against Tribulation is a long talk on how to bear trouble with faith and calm. This 1951 Sheed and Ward edition keeps the 1557 text whole while easing its old spelling, word order, and stale words for modern readers. Monica Stevens made the changes, and nothing was cut or added beyond small linking words.

The talk moves through fear, pain, loss, and death, testing each worry against reason and trust in God. Its slow, patient back-and-forth suits readers who want counsel rather than quick comfort. Even in plain modern dress, the work keeps its old voice: grave, kind, and firm about facing hard days without despair.
17592-a-narrative-of-the-expedition-to-d:
An American in the service of the Viceroy of Egypt wrote this narrative of the expedition to Dongola and Sennaar. It went under the command of Ismael Pasha, undertaken by order of Mehemmed Ali Pasha, Viceroy of Egypt. The book was published in London in 1822 by John Murray of Albemarle Street. Its author dedicates the work to Henry Salt, the British consul general in Egypt, calling him a fatherly friend in a foreign land.

The narrative was also recommended to the care of John William Bankes. Readers get an early eyewitness account of Egypt's southward expansion into Nubia and Sudan, by a participant. The book suits readers of African exploration and of Mehemmed Ali's Egypt.
17971-the-abolition-of-slavery-the-right:
William Lloyd Garrison and others put together this pamphlet on the abolition of slavery and the government's right under the war power. It opens with extracts from John Quincy Adams's speech of April 1842 on war with Britain and Mexico, and it argues from his words.

Adams held that Congress could not meddle with slavery in peace, but that war changed the case, since the nation's peace and welfare were at stake. The pamphlet presses that logic toward emancipation by war power. It is a short, sharp abolitionist tract, and a key text for readers who trace how the war power argument freed the slaves.
18392-thoughts-i-met-on-the-highway-word:
Ralph Waldo Trine, author of In Tune with the Infinite, published this book of friendly cheer in 1919 with Dodd, Mead in New York, copyrighted in 1912. Thoughts I Met on the Highway gathers selections from Trine's Life Books, one volume of selections for each week of the year. Trine's message runs through all his books: thoughts are forces, like builds like, and like attracts like.

The volume offers short pieces for the road: the winning of the best, the greatest thing ever known, every living creature, character building, and thought power. Trine writes for readers who want a daily lift, not a system: brief, warm counsels on living with courage, kindness, and hope. Readers get a pocket companion of New Thought: plain sentences meant to be read slowly, one a day, and carried onto the highway of ordinary life.
18531-timothy-s-quest-a-story-for-anybod:
Kate Douglas Wiggin wrote this story for anybody, young or old, who cares to read it. Wiggin also wrote The Birds' Christmas Carol and The Story of Patsy. Houghton, Mifflin published it in Boston and New York, with copyright in 1890. Timothy's Quest is told in scenes, like a play for the home, and the thirty-seventh thousand printing shows its long popularity.

Scene one gives Flossy Morrison learning the secret of death without ever having learned the secret of life. Scene two gives little Timothy Jessup assuming parental responsibilities. Later scenes show Timothy planning a campaign with providence assisting. Jabe Slocum acts as guardian angel. Timothy finds a house where he thinks a baby is needed, though the inmates do not entirely agree. Readers get a Wiggin tale of orphans, kindness, and a child's quest for a home.
18975-the-north-pole-its-discovery-in-19:
Robert E. Peary wrote this 1910 account of reaching the North Pole in 1909 under the Peary Arctic Club. Theodore Roosevelt wrote an introduction and Gilbert H. Grosvenor a foreword, and the book carries flags borne on the final dash. Peary sets his own trek inside a long history of polar tries.

He reviews Parry and other early explorers, then tells of ice, sledges, dogs, and the hard push north from a land base. Cold, drift, and open water test men and plans at each stage. Readers get the explorer's own case for his claim, plus a survey of how Arctic travel changed over time.
19156-the-continental-monthly-vol-iii-is:
This June 1863 issue of The Continental Monthly, devoted to literature and national policy, continues a defence of the Union in its second part. It contrasts the Union's upward path with the pro-slavery rebellion and its tendencies, tracing mankind's slow rise through revolution and faith toward a higher, more united life.

The writer argues that advancing civilisation multiplies and organises human bonds, while immoral, ignorant, indolent communities lapse toward disintegration and petty states. Such evil, he claims, corrects itself. Readers get a wartime Northern magazine essay, earnest, philosophical, and firm for Union.
19221-the-golden-treasury-of-the-best-so:
Francis Turner Palgrave selected this Golden Treasury of the best songs and lyrical poems in the English language, with pictures by A. Pearse. Dedicated to Alfred Tennyson, it recalls Henry Hallam, whose just judgment and patriotism Palgrave praises, and notes Tennyson's encouragement on walks at Treryn Dinas. The book aims to be a true national anthology.

Poems range from Drummond of Hawthornden on spring and love to Shakespeare on time and love, with lyrics chosen for beauty and lasting power. Readers get a classic anthology of English lyric verse across three centuries, still a fine introduction to the tradition.
19314-raphael-a-collection-of-fifteen-pi:
Estelle M. Hurll edited this 1899 art book on Raphael, with fifteen pictures and a portrait painted by himself. It opens with his character as an artist, books of reference, a directory of pictures, collateral reading, and a table of his life and contemporaries. Each picture then gets an introduction and reading.

Abraham and the Three Angels shows Abraham bowing low in Oriental robes, offering water, bread, and a calf under a tree, while Sarah peeps through a door at the mysterious guests. Hurll reads courtesy as honour craved, not favour given. Readers get a gentle guide to Raphael for home study.
19332-michael-angelo-buonarroti-with-tra:
Charles Holroyd, keeper of the National Gallery of British Art, wrote this 1903 life of Michelangelo, with translations of Condivi's life and three dialogues from the Portuguese by Francisco d'Ollanda. Plates show the David, the Pieta, the Battle of the Centaurs, and the Day of Judgment. The book is a scholarly tribute.

Young Michelangelo copies a faun so well that Lorenzo the Magnificent jokes that an old faun should lack teeth, so the boy cuts one tooth away and drills its root hole. Lorenzo then takes him into favour. Readers get a rich, illustrated life of a Renaissance master, artist, and man.
19470-yorkshire-lyrics-poems-written-in-:
John Hartley wrote this set of Yorkshire lyrics, in the dialect spoken in the West Riding, with a selection of fugitive verses in plain English added. Hartley, known for his Clock Almanack and Yorkshire Tales, writes of home life, work, and local characters in the voice of his county.

The dialect poems carry the book's heart: humor, pathos, and pride in Yorkshire speech. For readers outside the Riding, the verses offer both a glossary-free plunge into northern talk and a record of a spoken culture that print rarely caught.
19731-under-the-ocean-to-the-south-pole-:
Roy Rockwood was a house name for boys' adventure series books. Under the Ocean to the South Pole, from 1907, sends the submarine Wonder on a strange cruise. A scientist in the opening scene tightens bolts on a wild apparatus. He hopes aloud that the vessel will work as planned. His young friend Mark shares the doubt and the thrill.

Submarine polar voyages were fresh fantasy in 1907. No real submarine had yet cruised under polar ice. Rockwood's books mixed invention talk with constant peril. Storms, ice, and strange seas tested the young crew. Series readers returned for each new impossible trip. The Wonder books show early science fiction aimed squarely at boys.
1988-the-history-of-tom-thumb-to-which-a:
This old English chapbook tells the story of Tom Thumb, the tiny boy given to a childless ploughman and his wife by the magician Merlin. Set in the days of King Arthur, it follows a hero no bigger than a thumb through a world built for full-sized folk. Tom Thumb tales circulated for centuries in cheap print, passed from teller to teller before they reached books.

Tom survives scrapes with animals, courts, and kitchens, and two short tales follow: one of a cat and a mouse, and one of a cry of fire. The style is simple and direct, made for reading aloud to children. Children enjoy the scale jokes most, as Tom hides in puddings, rides mice, and outwits creatures far larger than himself.
20110-canada-the-empire-of-the-north-bei:
Agnes C. Laut published Canada: The Empire of the North in 1909. Her subtitle calls it the romantic story of Canada's growth. The book traces Canada from colony to kingdom, in her bold phrase. For twenty years, she notes, Canada's population barely grew at all.

Laut promises the tale itself will explain that long stall. She then asks what fast growth, like that in the United States, might bring. Tables of numbers sit beside tales of trade, fur, and settlement. Readers get a proud, sweeping history written when Canada's boom had just begun.
20617-young-wild-west-at-forbidden-pass-:
Young Wild West at Forbidden Pass is a dime novel of the West's favorite boy hero. Young Wild West leads his partners into danger at a mountain pass, and Arietta, his sweetheart, pays the toll of the title. The author signs himself simply An Old Scout.

The hero's portrait opens the tale. The flash in his eye tells of courage and persistence, while his athletic form shows strength and quickness. But his greatest quality is coolness and a fixed purpose to do right. Such dime novels filled railway stalls and boys' pockets across America, five cents at a time.
20791-for-love-of-country-a-story-of-lan:
A fair view holds young Seymour's heart in For Love of Country, an 1898 tale. The scene prints itself on his young mind with lasting force. Cyrus Townsend Brady sets his story of land and sea in the days of the American Revolution.

Sail and sword both serve the cause in Brady's rousing tale. Brady, a churchman and sea writer, loved tales of brave deeds. His heroes face British foes on deck and shore alike. The book shows how the Revolution was retold for young readers in the 1890s, as a call to love of country in stirring story form.
2125-the-nile-tributaries-of-abyssinia-a:
Samuel W. Baker explores the Nile tributaries of Abyssinia, now Ethiopia, and the sword hunters of the region, in a Victorian travel and hunting narrative. Baker sought the sources of the Nile and the game of the highlands. Baker, who had explored Ceylon, turned next to the Nile's highland feeders.

He describes rivers, tribes, and hunts with the energy of an adventurer, and his book joins his earlier Ceylon writings. Modern readers will enjoy the travel tale while weighing its colonial attitudes. The sword hunters, Arab traders with long blades, gave the book its second, stranger title.
21478-snow-shoes-and-canoes-or-the-early:
A fort in Hudson Bay needs winter stores in W. H. G. Kingston's Snow Shoes and Canoes. The stores lie at Fort Ross, some one hundred and fifty miles off. No canoes can be spared, so a party sets out overland to fetch them.

Bears, hunger, and deep weariness dog the march, told by a young fur trader. The party meets friendly and hostile Indigenous peoples along the way. Borrowed canoes later wreck in mighty rapids. Kingston drew on the true books of Ballantyne, who had served the Hudson's Bay Company, and made the matter his own.
22791-king-henry-v-arranged-for-represen:
Charles Kean arranged Shakespeare's King Henry V for performance at the Princess's Theatre, and this book prints his acting edition with historical and explanatory notes. The catalog record gives no year. Kean, the great Victorian actor-manager, was famous for productions that dressed Shakespeare in archaeology: every banner, shield, and costume researched.

The cast list shows the care and the era. The Earl of Westmoreland and the Archbishop of Canterbury head the roll. Sir Thomas Erpingham stands among the officers in King Henry's army. Bates and Nym, Falstaff's old followers turned soldiers, stand in the ranks, and the Boy is played by Miss Kate Terry. Kean's Henry V was a patriotic spectacle of the Crimean years. The edition preserves how Victorian London staged its favorite king.
22812-the-postal-service-of-the-united-s:
Erastus Granger, appointed postmaster at Buffalo Creek on September 30, 1804, opens this history of the United States postal service. Back then the nearest offices sat at Batavia, Erie, and Niagara, and mail moved slowly between scattered settlements. Granger himself was a second cousin of a leading political family of the day.

From such small beginnings the account traces how the post grew alongside the young nation. Local offices, routes, and officials anchor the story in real places and dates. Readers interested in how a country knits itself together will find the machinery here, shown one town at a time. The tone stays factual, closer to a record than a romance, and that plainness is part of its value.
22914-the-sceptical-chymist-or-chymico-p:
Robert Boyle argues with the alchemists in The Sceptical Chymist, printed in London by J. Crooke. Its full title promises chymico-physical doubts and paradoxes touching the spagyrists' principles, commonly called hypostatical, as proposed and defended by the generality of alchemists. A discourse on the same subject stands before the main work.

Boyle's target is the old doctrine that all matter springs from a few fixed principles like salt, sulfur, and mercury. Through dialogue and experiment he argues that claims must be tested, not inherited. The book, first issued in 1661, helped turn alchemy toward modern chemistry. Its spelling and style are of its century. Its demand for proof is the founding habit of laboratory science.
23340-campaigns-of-a-non-combatant-and-h:
George Alfred Townsend, a war correspondent, wrote this eighteen sixty six book of travel and report from the American Civil War and from Europe. As a non combatant, he saw camps, marches, and battles without bearing arms, and he writes as a witness rather than a soldier.

The chapters move from London in eighteen sixty three through war time scenes, with portraits of officers, camp life, and the press corps at work. Townsend dedicates the book to Miles O'Reilly, a fellow voice of the war, and his prose mixes road tales with sharp notes on men and events. Readers gain a reporter's view of war: close, mobile, and alert to both the grand sweep and the small human detail.
23450-the-book-of-ornamental-alphabets-a:
F. Delamotte collected and engraved this book of ornamental alphabets, ancient and medieval, from the eighth century onward, in a sixteenth edition printed in nineteen fourteen. Gothic, church text large and small, German arabesque, initials for illumination, monograms, crosses, and numerals fill the plates.

Delamotte, a draughtsman and engraver, aimed the book at architects, engineers, masons, decorative painters, lithographers, engravers, and carvers, at a modest price. His preface notes that no good cheap work on ancient alphabets then existed, after years of study in his trade. Designers and letter lovers will still value the plates as models, showing how letters can carry beauty, rank, and craft across a thousand years.
23547-sam-lambert-and-the-new-way-store-:
Published by the Grand Rapids Show Case Company in nineteen twelve, this book for clothiers and their clerks follows Sam Lambert, owner of the best clothing store in Medeena County. His corner shop faces the court house square, in a town with four clothing stores besides the Blue Front by the depot, with its cheap watches, guitar, accordions, and broken fiddle.

Sam, big boned and free hearted, just escaped a run for sheriff as too good natured for the gang and too fond of his store. He takes pride in his trade and keeps pace with ready to wear change. The book mixes story and sales counsel, showing how display, stock, and service win customers. Clothiers and readers of business history will enjoy Sam as a model merchant, brisk, honest, and awake to new ways.
24064-damned-if-you-don-t:
Randall Garrett published this short science-fiction story in Astounding Science Fiction in May 1960, with pictures by van Dongen. It opens on a workshop laboratory wrecked beyond use, where inventor Sam Bending surveys thousands of dollars of ruined equipment. The epigraph, borrowed from Lorenzo Dow, jokes about Calvinism: damned if you do, damned if you don't.

Garrett plays with a familiar tale, the wonderful invention that a great corporation or utility supposedly suppressed. Usually, the story notes, such an invention simply would not work, but here another twist waits. The result is a short, wry tale about inventors, backers, and the gap between a grand idea and a machine that runs.
24163-the-shepherd-of-banbury-s-rules-to:
John Claridge, shepherd of Banbury, wrote this weather book from forty years of experience, in a new edition printed in London in 1827. Its rules claim to tell the weather days ahead, and sometimes for months. They add a reasoned account of the causes of such changes, with the nature of wind, rain, snow, and more. Observation, not book learning, is its ground.

The introduction praises the luck of finding a trustworthy observer, since observing and reasoning upon observations are different things, and rarely do both fall to one man. Claridge warns against pedantry in deserts as in colleges, and against mistaking words for things. Readers get a practical country guide to reading the skies.
24218-the-works-of-samuel-johnson-ll-d-i:
This eighth volume of the Works of Samuel Johnson, published at Oxford in 1825, gathers his Lives of the English Poets. Its contents run from Prior, Congreve, Blackmore, Fenton, and Gay through Granville, Yalden, Tickell, Hammond, and Somervile. Later lives cover Savage, Swift, Broome, Pope, Pitt, Thomson, Watts, Philips, West, Collins, Dyer, Shenstone, Young, Mallet, Akenside, Gray, and Lyttelton.

The life of Matthew Prior opens the volume. Born July 21, 1664, by some accounts at Winburn in Dorsetshire and by others the son of a London joiner, Prior fell to his uncle. The uncle, a vintner near Charing Cross, sent him to Dr. Busby at Westminster. The Earl of Dorset found him reading Horace and paid for Cambridge. Readers get Johnson's brisk, judging lives of poets.
2474-the-circus-boys-on-the-flying-rings:
Edgar B. P. Darlington's Circus Boys on the Flying Rings follows two boys making their start in the circus, learning the trapeze and the flying rings under the big top. The story mixes training, rivalry, and show-day thrills, with the boys' pluck carrying them from beginners to performers. Darlington writes the circus from the inside, with sawdust and spangles.

The book launched a series beloved by young readers of its era. Its energy and its detail of circus life charm still. Boys' adventure fans will find a lively opener.
24856-odysseus-the-hero-of-ithaca-adapte:
Mary E. Burt and Zenaide A. Ragozin adapted Odysseus, the Hero of Ithaca, from a Greek schoolbook, published by Scribner in 1898. The tale follows the hero from Troy to home: Paris sails to Greece, Helen flees, the Greeks sail for Troy, and the city falls. Then comes the long return, past Calypso's isle to Circe, who turns his men to swine.

Odysseus alone resists her magic wine, sword in hand, and wins her oath not to harm him. Burt and Ragozin tell the epic in plain chapters for school use, keeping its loyalty and bravery to the fore. The book gives young readers a clear, stirring door into Homer's Odyssey.
252-copyright-law-of-the-united-states-o:
Title 17 of the United States Code sets the law of copyright, and this file gives it in full. The Copyright Act of 1976, sections 101 through 810, opens with definitions of works, authors, and copies. Sections on fair use, libraries, and duration follow.

The file's note flags sections 106, 107, and 108 as of special interest to information users. Lawyers, librarians, and publishers consult the act to judge rights and limits. Its plain text form suits searching and citation. The act still frames American copyright today. Later amendments built on this act, but its structure remains the base.
25232-the-history-of-england-from-the-ac:
This volume of the Political History of England covers the reign of George III from his accession, in a series meant to carry English history beyond Lingard's work, which ended in 1688. Twelve volumes were planned, built on modern research and written for general readers as well as students.

The narrative follows the young king and his tutor, the Earl of Bute, made groom of the stole in 1756. Bute taught George that a king should govern directly, drawing on Bolingbroke's Idea of a Patriot King and Blackstone's Commentaries. The volume opens the story of a reign that would lose America and remake Britain.
25465-skippy-bedelle-his-sentimental-pro:
Owen Johnson follows Skippy Bedelle from urchin to complete man of the world in this Lawrenceville story. Until his first great disillusions, Skippy regards the feminine sex as unmitigated nuisances and wonders at the Creator's hidden purposes. Two inventions mark his youth: the Bedelle Foot Regulator and mosquito-proof socks, both of which bring a new sentimental need for consolation.

Later Skippy falls for Miss Lafontaine, opening his heart and spreading his inventive treasures before her. She passes lightly over the improved bathtub but loves the mosquito-proof stockings, and with her faith he can wait years for his chance. Little, Brown published the book at Boston in 1937, from a copyright of 1922, illustrated by Ernest Fuhr.
25830-a-discourse-of-a-method-for-the-we:
René Descartes sets out his method for guiding reason and finding truth in the sciences, in a London printing of 1649. The translator hails Descartes as first among the thinkers of his age and likens his own rendering to a copy of a fine painting, rough yet true to the design. The discourse itself urges readers to trust only what reason sees with clear proof.

Senses and fancy, Descartes warns, can mislead. The sun looks small and the stars look near. A mind can picture a lion head on a goat body without proving such a beast lives. Whether waking or dreaming, we should yield only to the proof of reason. The book thus lays the ground rules for modern inquiry, doubt first, then sure steps.
27210-the-surprising-adventures-of-bampf:
The Surprising Adventures of Bampfylde Moore Carew, King of the Beggars, in the 1850s Allman edition, tells the life of an extraordinary man, with a dictionary of the cant language. Carew was born in July 1693, son of the Reverend Theodore Carew, rector of Bickley near Tiverton in Devon.

His godfathers, Hugh Bampfylde and Major Moore, contended for president at his splendid baptism, settling it by tossing a coin. Carew's career among beggars, disguises, and cant speech made him a legend, and the book preserves his tricks, his language, and his luck.
27341-mother-earth-vol-1-no-4-june-1906-:
The June 1906 fourth number of Mother Earth, a monthly magazine from New York devoted to social science and literature, opens with a poem by Viroqua Daniels on Mrs. Grundy, the figure of narrow custom who rules speech, play, and belief from childhood on. Emma Goldman published the magazine, and the issue carries her own letter beside pieces by Alexander Berkman and others.

Inside, readers find a piece on Henrik Ibsen, Friedrich Nietzsche on the Antichrist, Peter Kropotkin on brain work and manual work, and Henriette Fuerth on motherhood and marriage. Trade-union tactics, war, and government control get the same plain treatment. The issue gives a clear view of radical thought in 1906, in short essays and poems meant to be read and argued over.
27704-memoirs-of-the-court-and-cabinets-:
The Duke of Buckingham and Chandos compiled this second volume of memoirs of the court and cabinets of George III from original family documents, published in London in 1853. It covers the years 1788 through 1794 and beyond.

Its contents run from the king's illness and the regency question through Pitt's budgets, the French Revolution, and the war with France. Built from letters and papers rather than a single narrative, the volume gives an insider's view of ministers, princes, and Parliament in crisis. Later sections cover the king's recovery, Irish promotions, and dissensions within the royal family.
28632-a-plea-for-the-criminal-being-a-re:
The Reverend J. L. A. Kayll's A Plea for the Criminal, printed by W. Smith of Invercargill in 1905, answers Dr. Chapple's Fertility of the Unfit. Kayll, a corresponding member of the Howard Association, explains the leading principles of criminological and reformatory science. His authorities span Brockway of Elmira, Dugdale, Havelock Ellis, Ferri, Garofalo, Krafft-Ebing, Lacassagne, and Tallack.

Chapters treat elimination as Chapple proposed it, society's obligations toward the weak, the new penology, and prevention of crime. American experiments at Elmira close the argument before a conclusion. Kayll asks readers to understand the criminal, why he is one, and what chances remain to him, without shutting eyes to shocking crime. Readers get an Edwardian plea for charity with intelligence.
28744-ballads-of-robin-hood-and-other-ou:
Selected and edited by Frank Sidgwick, this volume gathers old English ballads about Robin Hood and other outlaws. It is the fourth set in his Popular Ballads of the Olden Time series, printed in London by Sidgwick and Jackson. The ballads are presented as traditional songs whose makers are unknown, passed down by singers long before they reached print.

The contents follow Robin Hood through encounters with a monk, a potter, and Guy of Gisborne, and end with his death. Other outlaw tales stand beside his, including Adam Bell, Clym of the Clough, and William of Cloudesly, plus Johnny o' Cockley's Well and Sir Andrew Barton. Readers get the outlaw legend in its old verse form, rough, direct, and full of ambush, disguise, and forest justice.
28858-the-heptameron-of-margaret-queen-o:
Edited by David Widger, this linked index covers the Project Gutenberg edition of the Heptameron, the story collection of Margaret, Queen of Navarre. Translated by George Saintsbury, the Heptameron gathers tales told over seven days by travelers, in the manner of Boccaccio. The index lists all five volumes, with the prologue, each day's tales, appendices, and the pictures that illustrate them.

The first day's tales alone show the collection's range: a proctor of Alençon, a muleteer's wife who dies rather than yield her chastity, and the revenge of the Queen of Naples. The index lets a reader find any tale by day and number, and follow the illustrations beside the text. It serves as a map to one of the great story books of the French Renaissance.
28969-the-illustrated-works-of-friedrich:
David Widger edited this linked index to the illustrated works of Friedrich Schiller, who lived from 1759 to 1805. The index covers his histories, the Thirty Years War and the Revolt of the Netherlands. His plays include The Robbers, Fiesco, Love and Intrigue, the Wallenstein trilogy, Wilhelm Tell, Don Carlos, Demetrius, Mary Stuart, and The Maid of Orleans.

His poems in three periods, his aesthetical essays and philosophical letters, and his novel The Ghost Seer appear as well. The Robbers chapters alone run through five acts, from a tavern on the Saxon frontier to the Bohemian woods. Readers get a map to Schiller's whole shelf in English, play by play and poem by poem, useful for students of German classic literature.
29063-a-historical-survey-of-the-customs:
John Hoyland published this survey in York in 1816, after watching Romani families living in great poverty in Northamptonshire, Bedfordshire, and Hertfordshire. Calling them by the period name Gypsies, Hoyland set out to trace their origin, describe their customs and habits, and argue for improving their condition.

Twelve sections move from the people's history and language to their trades, travels, and treatment by settled society. Hoyland writes as a reformer, not just an observer: he wants readers to see hardship they could help relieve. Readers get an early nineteenth-century study of a people little understood by their neighbors, valuable both for its facts and for its humane, if dated, point of view.
29189-a-letter-from-a-clergyman-to-his-f:
This Augustan Reprint Society volume, number 143, reprints an anonymous 1726 letter from a clergyman to his friend, giving an account of the travels of Captain Lemuel Gulliver. Martin Kallich supplies the introduction. The letter is a contemporary response to Jonathan Swift's Gulliver's Travels, published the same year.

Read as a period document, the letter shows how Swift's satire landed with its first readers: what they took literally, what they laughed at, and what they questioned. Kallich's notes place the piece in its publishing history. Readers get a small but telling artifact of eighteenth-century reading, a friend's letter about a book that had just startled London.
29461-preliminary-specifications-program:
Digital Equipment Corporation issued these preliminary specifications in October 1960 for the Programmed Data Processor Model Three, the PDP-3. The manual describes a stored-program, general-purpose digital machine that works in parallel on 36-bit numbers, with a single address and a single instruction form. Its sections cover the central processor, storage, and standard input and output gear.

Engineers will find operating speeds, instruction formats, number systems, indexing, indirect addressing, and a full instruction list, down to ten-microsecond add and subtract times. The text is terse and exact, made for builders and buyers, not for casual reading. Historians of early computing get a sharp snapshot of a machine built just as small computers began to spread.
30727-motor-boat-boys-down-the-coast-or-:
Louis Arundel writes Motor Boat Boys Down the Coast, subtitled Through Storm and Stress to Florida, copyrighted in 1913 by M. A. Donohue of Chicago. Arundel, author of Motor Boat Boys on the St. Lawrence, down the Mississippi, on the Great Lakes, and among the Florida Keys, opens with afloat on the lower Delaware.

Later chapters add a good omen for the start, Jack taking a hydro-aeroplane message, the first camp fire ashore, and a storm with no refuge in sight. A close shave with no damage, the motor boat flotilla going to sea, and the camp invaded follow. A frontispiece shows Jack crouching, elbow on knee, taking careful aim. Arundel writes a brisk boys' boating adventure.
31009-if-at-first-you-don-t:
John Brudy's short science fiction story, printed in Amazing Stories in June 1960, centers on Amos Jordan, Secretary for Cislunar Navigation, and his deputy Clements. Their problem is '58 Beta, the first long-lived satellite of the old Vanguard series, now due to fall from orbit while crowds of newer satellites already crowd the sky.

Jordan wants the worn-out craft gone as a menace to navigation. Public feeling pulls the other way, with some voices urging that it burn up and others that it be saved for a museum. The story turns a routine policy choice into a wry look at sentiment, monuments, and the clutter left behind by early spaceflight.
31075-in-the-ranks-from-the-wilderness-t:
The Reverend R. E. M'Bride's 1881 memoir tells the Civil War as seen by a private soldier in the Army of the Potomac, from the Wilderness to Appomattox Court House. M'Bride had been a mere boy when he enlisted, and he writes with warm memory of comrades who showed kindness and forbearance to the young soldier in their ranks.

His preface hopes the book will carry military tradition to a generation grown up since the war, through stories told at home rather than formal histories alone. The result is a ground-level account of marching, fighting, and camp life in the war's final year, valued for its modesty, humor, and firsthand detail.
31081-the-german-classics-v-20-masterpie:
Held here is volume twenty of The German Classics, masterpieces of German literature translated into English. It is in the patron's edition in twenty volumes, published by the German Publication Society in New York in 1914. Its authors include Jakob Wassermann, Bernhard Kellermann, Max Halbe, Hugo von Hofmannsthal, Arthur Schnitzler, Frank Wedekind, and Ernst Hardt. Its frontispiece is The Warden of Paradise, from a painting by Franz von Stuck.

A special essay by Mrs. Amelia von Ende covers the contemporary German drama. Translators include Paul H. Grummann on Mother Earth, Bayard Quincy Morgan on The Marriage of Sobeide, John Heard, Jr., on Tristram the Jester, and Katharine Royce on God's Beloved. They end with Albert Wilhelm Boesche on The Court Singer. It is the closing volume of a great translated library.
31248-a-little-garrison-a-realistic-nove:
Fritz von der Kyrburg's realistic novel of German army life, translated and edited by Wolf von Schierbrand and published by Frederick A. Stokes in January 1904, opens at an evening party at Captain König's, where Frau Clara König arranges her musical soirée with careful hands. Ten chapters follow a casino dance, the consequences of a May bowl, the case of Sergeant Schmitz, officers at a masquerade, and a sensational event stirring the garrison.

Later chapters watch an airy structure collapse, changes in the garrison, and resignations in order, closing with unto this last. Written by a serving lieutenant under a pen name, the novel scandalized readers with its frank picture of officers' manners, debts, and honor.
31783-was-general-thomas-slow-at-nashvil:
Henry V. Boynton's 1896 book, in a limited edition of 450 copies, defends General George H. Thomas against the charge that he was slow at Nashville. Its preface says a recent revival of that venerable charge led to an article in the New York Sun of August 9, 1896, reproduced here with a few brief additions.

Boynton also presents, in concise form, the outlines of General James H. Wilson's cavalry operations at Nashville and in his campaign through Alabama and Georgia, movements he calls without parallel in the war. Readers get a veteran's rebuttal and a compact campaign history, written while the arguments of the Civil War were still alive.
32958-edge-hill-the-battle-and-battlefie:
Edwin A. Walford's Edge Hill: The Battle and Battlefield gives a detailed account of the first great battle of the English Civil War, with notes on Banbury and thereabout. It is a second edition of 1904. Walford notes that the plans of battle in this edition resemble two from his 1886 book, then the first diagrammatic representations of the fight. He adds new facts, inferences, and letters from Captain Nathaniel Fiennes and Captain Kightley, reproduced with the help of Oxford and Birmingham libraries.

The book suits walkers and students who want to see a battlefield as well as read about it. It matches ground to troop movements and to the town that served the armies. Its diagrams, letters, and local notes make the seventeenth-century fight feel near. As local history it is careful and concrete, and it preserves the work of a writer who knew both the field and the archives.
33376-a-vindication-of-england-s-policy-:
C. R. Haines's vindication, published in London in 1884, defends England's policy on the opium trade between India and China. Haines writes that about two years before, he had gone thoroughly into the question, and his preface sets out the case for a policy much attacked at home. His argument weighs trade, revenue, and Chinese demand against charges of immorality and greed.

The pamphlet suits readers of Victorian imperial history, offering the official case in its own terms. Its tone is legal and reasoned, not rhetorical, and its detail on India-China trade remains useful. For students of the opium question, it is a key source: a contemporary defence, stated plainly, of a policy that history has judged harshly.
33737-the-curtezan-unmasked-or-the-whore:
A spiritual physician prescribed this moral tract in London in 1664, printed for Henry Marsh at the Prince's Arms in Chancery Lane. The Curtezan Unmasked, or The Whoredomes of Jezebel Painted to the Life, opens with Proverbs: the lips of a strange woman drop as a honeycomb. Proverbs continues: her end is bitter as wormwood and sharp as a two-edged sword. Its author promises antidotes against lust, or heavenly julips to cool men in fever.

The tract paints its subject as a beautiful siren with a woman's face ending in a serpent's tail, an unsatiable harpy whose cruel talons hide beneath her wings. It urges readers to bolt the door upon her as Amnon did upon Tamar. For historians of sexuality, preaching, and Restoration popular print, the pamphlet preserves the fierce, vivid rhetoric of seventeenth-century moral reform.
33820-an-architect-s-note-book-in-spain-:
M. Digby Wyatt, Slade Professor of Fine Art at Cambridge, records Spanish domestic architecture in this note-book, with one hundred of his own sketches reproduced by the autotype process. Dedicated to Owen Jones, his brother in art, the book grew from a first visit to Spain in the autumn of 1869. Wyatt then resolved to see and draw as much architectural remains as time and means allowed, publishing sketches and notes in the precise form in which they were made.

Wyatt feared that Spain's glorious past was being trampled out day by day, and that minor monuments of art would rapidly disappear whatever the country's future fortunes. His note-book therefore preserves houses, courtyards, details, and ornament that might otherwise be lost. Architects, historians, and lovers of Spain will value a visual record made on the spot by a sympathetic, skilled observer.
34044-bee-hunting-a-book-of-valuable-inf:
John R. Lockard wrote this handbook on bee hunting, published at Columbus, Ohio, in 1908 by A. R. Harding. Lockard, born in a mountain valley and a bee hunter for forty years, tells how to line bees to their trees. Chapters cover early spring hunting, bees watering, hunting from sumac and buckwheat, and fall hunting.

Later chapters treat baits and scents, the line of flight, cutting the tree and moving the bees, and customs and ownership of wild bees. Lockard writes from a lifetime in timbered hills full of game. The book still guides readers who follow wild bees.
34093-mink-trapping-a-book-of-instructio:
A. R. Harding edited this book of instruction on mink trapping, published at Columbus, Ohio, in 1906. It gives many methods for trappers, from general information and mink habits to the size and care of skins, good and lasting baits, and bait and scent. Places to set, Indian methods, and trapping on the prairie follow.

Southern and northern methods, unusual ways, salt sets, log sets, deadfalls, and steel traps round out the book, with points for the young trapper. Pictures show mink, trappers' shacks, streams, and catches. The book preserves the mink trapper's craft in plain terms.
34172-peter-s-rock-in-mohammed-s-flood-f:
Thomas W. Allies wrote this seventh volume of The Formation of Christendom, from Saint Gregory the Great to Saint Leo the Third. It appeared in London in 1890 by Burns and Oats and in New York by the Catholic Publication Society. A prologue gathers the titles of the fifty-six chapters of all seven volumes, each meant to stand alone yet link in a chain.

Allies sees the Church as a vast kingdom whose deeds are parts of something far greater, with evidence of doctrine and works piling up over time. Narrow views, he warns, shrink the gigantic to the puny. The volume offers a Catholic history of early medieval Christendom.
3483-widger-s-quotations-from-the-projec:
David Widger gathered this file of quotations from William Dean Howells, the fourth in his series of quotation books for Project Gutenberg. It collects short passages from Howells's novels, essays, and criticism, rather than telling a single story. A reader can open it at any point and hear Howells on American life, books, and manners in a few lines.

Howells, long called the dean of American letters, wrote with calm realism about middle class people and their choices. These extracts show his gentle irony and his care for ordinary speech. The file works as a sampler for readers new to Howells and as a quick source of lines, while his novels give the full stories behind them.
3493-widger-s-quotations-from-the-projec:
David Widger gathered this file of quotations from Oliver Wendell Holmes Senior, the fifth in his series of quotation books for Project Gutenberg. Holmes, a Boston doctor, poet, and essayist, wrote the Breakfast Table series and many poems. This file collects short passages from his work for readers who want his wit in brief form.

The extracts show Holmes on medicine, books, Boston life, and human nature, with the talkative charm that made him famous. A reader can browse a page or two and catch his style without starting a long essay. The file works as a sampler, while his full essays and poems give the arguments and stories behind these lines.
3531-widger-s-quotations-from-the-projec:
David Widger gathered this file of quotations from Lord Chesterfield, the sixth in his series of quotation books for Project Gutenberg. Chesterfield, an eighteenth century statesman, is best known for letters of advice to his son on manners, conduct, and the art of pleasing in society. This file lifts short passages from his writing for quick reading.

Readers meet Chesterfield's polished, worldly voice in brief form: counsel on politeness, study, and self command, mixed with the snobbery of his age. The set works as a sampler for those curious about Georgian manners and as a source of short lines. His full letters give the longer arguments behind these extracts.
3542-widger-s-quotations-from-the-projec:
David Widger gathered this file of quotations from Giacomo Casanova, the seventh in his series of quotation books for Project Gutenberg. Casanova, the Venetian adventurer of the eighteenth century, wrote famous memoirs of love, travel, gambling, and escape. This file lifts short passages from his work for browsing, rather than retelling his long life story.

Readers meet Casanova's worldly wit in brief form: remarks on women, fortune, freedom, and the pleasures of a life lived boldly. The set works as a sampler for those curious about the man behind the legend. His full memoirs give the adventures, prisons, and disguises that these short lines only hint at.
3603-widger-s-quotations-from-the-projec:
David Widger gathered this file of quotations from Guy de Maupassant, the eighth in his series of quotation books for Project Gutenberg. Maupassant, the French master of the short story, wrote with sharp irony about peasants, officials, soldiers, and lovers in Norman France. This file lifts short passages from his work for browsing, rather than retelling his tales.

Readers meet Maupassant's bleak wit in brief form: remarks on greed, vanity, and the surprises of fate. The set works as a sampler for those new to his stories and as a source of short lines. His full stories, such as The Necklace and Boule de Suif, give the plots and twists that these extracts only suggest.
3626-widger-s-quotations-from-the-projec:
David Widger gathered this file of quotations from Abraham Lincoln's writings, the tenth in his series of quotation books for Project Gutenberg. Lincoln, the sixteenth president of the United States, wrote speeches, letters, and messages that became classics of American prose. This file lifts short passages from those writings for browsing, rather than retelling his life.

Readers meet Lincoln's plain, biblical voice in brief form: remarks on union, slavery, democracy, and the duties of war. The set works as a sampler for students and speakers and as a source of short lines. His full speeches and letters give the occasions and arguments behind these famous sentences.
3661-widger-s-quotations-from-the-projec:
David Widger gathered this file of quotations from the Essays of Montaigne, the twelfth in his series of quotation books for Project Gutenberg. Montaigne, the French essayist of the sixteenth century, wrote about himself to understand mankind, and his sentences on custom, death, friendship, and judgment have been quoted ever since. This file lifts short passages from his essays for browsing.

Readers meet Montaigne's modest, skeptical voice in brief form: remarks that test grand claims against daily life. The set works as a sampler for those new to the essays and as a source of short lines. The full essays, in many volumes, give the stories and digressions behind these famous sentences.
3730-widger-s-quotations-from-the-projec:
David Widger gathered this quote book from the long court memoirs of France, picking lines that stand on their own. The entries run from Louis the Fourteenth and Madame de Maintenon to the Duke of Saint-Simon, and they catch vanity, piety, fear, and wit in a single sentence each. One line notes a queen who never knew a happy day, another a king who wept while still a king.

The collection suits browsing, since no entry needs its neighbors to make sense, and each page jumps from one court to another. Readers hunting for a sharp remark on power, marriage, or faith will find plenty to copy into a commonplace book. It also serves as a sampler for the great memoirs themselves, pointing back to Saint-Simon and his fellows for the full stories.
4704-nomads-of-the-north-a-story-of-roma:
James Oliver Curwood opens Nomads of the North in late March, at the dying out of the Eagle Moon. Neewa the black bear cub gets his first real look at the world. His mother Noozak, old and rheumatic, slept four months that winter instead of three. Neewa, born while she slept, was over two months old, not six weeks, when they left the den. Noozak chose a cavern at a high, barren ridge crest, and Neewa first looked down into a valley.

Coming out of darkness into sunlight, Neewa was blinded for a time, hearing, smelling, and feeling many things before he could see. From that den begins a story of romance and adventure under open stars, following bear and humans through northern seasons. Readers get a warm animal adventure for young and old, with Curwood's love of wild life, and a cub's eye view of a hard, beautiful world.
4991-the-pony-rider-boys-in-new-mexico-o:
Four boys calling themselves the Pony Rider Boys ride into New Mexico in this western adventure, and even strangers in a rail car have heard of their lively stunts. Two men whisper about the boys behind them, one snoring in the seat, wondering whether kids out for a holiday could really be as tough as report says.

The answer comes on plains and mountains, as the boys chase the end of the silver trail through scrapes and dangers. The catalog record leaves the author unnamed. Readers get a boys' western of horses, humor, and teamwork, where youth itself becomes a kind of courage on the trail.
5204-the-inns-and-taverns-of-pickwick-wi:
B. W. Matz's study follows the inns and taverns of Dickens's Pickwick Papers through the coaching age. Chapters visit the Golden Cross at Charing Cross, the Bull at Rochester, the White Hart in the Borough, La Belle Sauvage, the Leather Bottle at Cobham. The Town Arms at Eatanswill appears among many others.

Matz pairs each inn with its scene in the novel and with its later history, using engravings and local records. The book serves both Dickens readers, who want to walk Pickwick's road. Students of old English inns get their share too: how coaching houses lived, changed, and sometimes vanished.
6131-wonders-of-creation-a-descriptive-a:
Wonders of Creation gives a popular account of volcanoes and their phenomena, meant for the young in 1872. Its epigraph from Nahum pictures mountains quaking, hills melting, and earth burning at divine presence, while the preface avoids scientific detail and philosophical speculation.

A reading of the pages may so stir youthful curiosity that some, on reaching riper years, will inquire more deeply into volcanic agency, its causes, and modes of operation. Some may even climb nearer active volcanoes and examine phenomena themselves. The book treats fire mountains as marvels meant to wake inquiry.
6357-snowflakes-and-sunbeams-or-the-youn:
R. M. Ballantyne plunges his reader into arctic winter and the wilderness of North America, introducing the chief persons of his tale. An old fur trader tries to fix his son's flint and finds it harder than expected. A counting room scene follows, and a wolf hunt in the prairies lets Charley astonish his father and break in a new horse. Peter Mactavish turns amateur doctor, Charley tells Kate his views, and Kate grows sagacious.

Spring brings voyageurs, a store, farewell to Kate, and Charley's departure with the brigade as a voyageur. The voyage, encampment, and surprise follow, with sporting beginnings, whisky John caught, and a storm. Ballantyne gives boys a northern life of snow, trade, and hard travel, told with the cheerful detail of a man who knows the country.
6714-dave-dashaway-and-his-hydroplane-or:
Roy Rockwood sends Dave Dashaway aloft in a hydroplane for daring adventures over the Great Lakes. The tale opens at an aero meet in Columbus, where a messenger boy stares in wonder at a great prize monoplane in its hangar. The man in charge, one-armed, limping, scarred like a war veteran, takes the telegram for Dave.

From that hangar, Dave flies into contests, rescues, and scrapes over lake and shore, with pluck as his chief fuel. Rockwood keeps the pace fast and the talk boyish. Dave Dashaway and His Hydroplane is a breezy, early aviation book for boys, full of machines, nerve, and lake air.
7123-home-vegetable-gardening-a-complete:
F F Rockwell writes Home Vegetable Gardening as a complete and practical guide to planting and care of all vegetables, fruits, and berries worth growing for home use. The author of Around the Year in the Garden and Gardening Indoors and Under Glass addresses two classes. Some garden as a hobby, while others, in days of high prices, find it a great help. Many in both classes have narrow experience and limited spare time.

The book serves as first aid to such gardeners, who want practical, efficient work with the least fuss and loss of time. Rockwell notes garden books seldom lack information, yet often fail to present it in the clearest way. His guide therefore orders each crop plainly, from planting to table, for the home gardener.
7321-the-nibelungenlied-translated-into-:
George Henry Needler, associate professor of German at University College, Toronto, translates the Nibelungenlied into rhymed English verse in the metre of the original. His preface states a simple purpose: to place one of the world's great epic poems within reach of English readers. Translations are at best poor substitutes for originals, he admits, and a new version implies a criticism of those before it.

Needler's apology rests on metre: no earlier English version, he argues, reproduced the original's metrical form, and his hope is to make the poem's outlines clear in its own music. The epic of Siegfried, Kriemhild, and Burgundian doom thus gains an English shape that honours its German verse. Scholars and general readers share the gain.
7962-over-the-top-by-an-american-soldier:
Arthur Guy Empey, an American machine gunner who served in France, wrote this memoir of trench warfare, adding Tommy's Dictionary of the Trenches and sixteen illustrations and diagrams. Dedicated to his mother and sister, it draws on sixteen years of rough living around the world. Before the mast and in the trenches, and on close observation of the peoples he met. The foreword presents the book as experience, not book learning.

Empey describes raids, bombardments, and daily trench routine in a soldier's direct voice, and his dictionary explains the slang of the line. The book was widely read in wartime America and helped civilians picture the Western Front. It remains a vivid first-hand account of the war as ordinary soldiers endured it.
8447-morien-a-metrical-romance-rendered-:
Jessie L. Weston renders Morien, a medieval Dutch Arthurian romance, into English prose, with designs by Caroline Watts. The volume is number four in her series of Arthurian romances retold in modern prose, following her versions of Sir Gawain and the Green Knight and others. Morien, a knight of Arthur's court, undertakes quests in the chivalric world Weston loved.

Weston, a scholar of Arthurian legend whose work later influenced T. S. Eliot, made medieval romances readable for a general audience. Readers get a knightly tale in clear prose, with an introduction and notes placing it in the Arthurian tradition. It suits anyone entering Arthurian literature beyond Malory, through a scholar's retelling.
9078-sanders-union-fourth-reader-embraci:
Charles Sanders wrote this school reader for American common schools, as the fourth step in his Union series. It moves pupils from easy reading in the Third Reader to harder work in the Fifth. A full account of the rules of reading aloud sits at its heart. Prose and poetry pieces serve as practice.

Sanders notes that most pupils left school before they reached higher readers, so he made this volume count. Exercises vary in style and are graded for teaching in schools of every grade. The book now shows how nineteenth-century America taught children not just to read, but to speak text aloud with skill.
9480-in-the-heart-of-the-vosges-and-othe:
Miss Betham-Edwards, an English writer on France, published In the Heart of the Vosges in 1911, a book of travel sketches. She calls herself a devious traveller, drawn to spots off the main road, and claims many of her French scenes had no English account before. The sketches range from the Vosges hills to Toulouse, Provins, and small towns in Alsace. Plates add views of the places she walks.

Chapters linger in Gérardmer, climb to shrines, meet lady merchants and socialist mayors, and note local craft and speech. Betham-Edwards writes with warmth and a sharp eye for custom, church, and town life. A reader gets a slow, fond tour of unfrequented France, just before the Great War changed the border lands for good.
9569-mountain-pictures-and-other-poems-p:
Part two of volume two of Whittier's works continues his Poems of Nature with Mountain Pictures. Franconia from the Pemigewasset and Monadnock from Wachuset open the run, praising northern peaks in golden light. The Vanishers, The Pageant, and The Pressed Gentian follow, with A Mystery, A Sea Dream, and Hazel Blossoms. Sunset on the Bearcamp and The Seeking of the Waterfall close the early run.

Whittier asks the mountains for calm and strength, and finds his common life lifted by their shapes and hues. His verse stays plain, devout, and rooted in New England ground. A reader gets Whittier's mountain lyrics at their finest, with peaks, falls, and flowers as signs of a steady order.
a-friend-of-c-sar-a-tale-of-the-fall-of-: William Stearns Davis tells of a friend of Caesar in the fall of the Roman Republic, from 50 to 47 before Christ. Its chapters visit Praeneste, the upper walks of society, and the privilege of a vestal. Pompeius Magnus, Lucius Ahenobarbus, and Greek meeting Roman fill the tale. Davis writes historical fiction grounded in the politics of Rome's last republican years.
a-handbook-to-agra-and-the-taj-sikandra-: Ernest Binfield Havell gives a handbook to Agra and the Taj, Sikandra, and Fatehpur Sikri. A historical introduction traces the great Moguls from Babar through Akbar, Jahangir, Shah Jahan, and Aurangzeb. The guide then describes the fort, mosques, tombs, baths, and gates of Agra. Havell writes for travelers who wish to understand Mogul art and history.
a-narrative-of-the-expedition-to-dongola: George Bethune English, an American serving the Viceroy of Egypt, narrates the expedition to Dongola and Sennaar under Ismael Pasha, ordered by Mehemmed Ali Pasha. Arriving at the camp at Wady Halfa on the Second Cataract, he found about four thousand troops. Turkish cavalry, infantry, and artillery stood alongside Bedouin horsemen and Mogrebin foot soldiers.
