Some one hundred and twenty large boats travelled in company, and the account follows the column upriver from that crowded starting point.
a-new-hochelagan-burying-ground-discover: William Douw Lighthall reports the discovery of a prehistoric burying ground at Westmount, on the Westmount slope of Mount Royal in Montreal, found between July and September 1898. The four or five graves found so far lay scattered at considerable intervals. He provisionally links them to the people of old Hochelaga and their Mohawk neighbours, whose exact relationship remained unascertained, and the notes were privately printed for the writer.
a-unique-story-of-a-marvellous-career-li:
Joel Benton writes the life of Phineas T. Barnum, the American showman, from his birth and school days in Connecticut to the height of his fame. The contents open with his first visit to New York, farm work, and store keeping. They follow his many ventures. Among them are a lottery business, a newspaper, and a libel suit that jailed him.

The story proper begins when Barnum finds his calling: the purchase of Joice Heth, a traveling circus, then the American Museum in New York. Giants and dwarfs, Tom Thumb's triumphs in London and France, and Jenny Lind fill the later chapters. Benton tells it all with anecdotes and admiration for Barnum's energy.
a-voyage-of-consolation-being-in-the-nat: Sara Jeannette Duncan, writing as Mrs Everard Cotes, offers a voyage of consolation as a sequel to the experiences of An American Girl in London. Published by Appleton at New York, illustrated and priced at a dollar and fifty cents, the novel continues a heroine's travels after London. Its list of the author's uniform edition runs from His Honour and a Lady to A Daughter of To-Day. The list places the sequel among a career of Anglo-American social comedy.
collins-the-truth-about-lynching-and-the:
The Truth About Lynching and the Negro in the South, by Winfield H. Collins, was published by the Neale Publishing Company of New York in 1918. Its subtitle states its plea without disguise: that the South be made safe for the white race. Collins, who also wrote on the domestic slave trade, dates his preface from Reids Grove, Maryland, January 30, 1918.

Chapter I traces lynching before the Civil War. The word is derived from a Virginia farmer named Lynch, who kept order in his section during the Revolutionary War. Early punishments, Collins argues, ran to riding the rail, whipping, and tar and feathers, seldom to death. Later chapters plead his case through courtroom reports, including an arson trial at Chestertown, Maryland.
copyright-law-of-the-united-states-of-am:
The hosted text is the Copyright Law of the United States as compiled in Title 17 of the United States Code, issued through the Copyright Office. It is the statute itself, chapter by chapter. Early chapters define what can be protected, from books and music to pictures, programs, and buildings, and say who owns a work, how long protection lasts, and how ownership passes.

Later chapters cover registration and deposit, the notice once required on copies, and what counts as infringement, with the fair use section that teachers, critics, and parodists rely on. Others handle record keeping, fees, the Copyright Royalty Judges, and protection for boat hull designs and chip masks. Dry as it reads, this is the rulebook behind American publishing and film.
crusaders-of-new-france-a-chronicle-of-t:
A history of French Canada by William Bennett Munro fills this 1918 volume, the fourth in the Chronicles of America series. Its subtitle calls it a chronicle of the fleur-de-lis in the wilderness. Munro inscribes it to Father Henri Beaudé, in honour of the men of his race and faith.

Eleven chapters run from Bourbon France to the daily life of the colonists. The founding of New France, the iron governor, and La Salle and the voyageurs take the centre. Then come the church, the seigneurs, and the coureurs-de-bois. Trade, farms, and home life close the tale. Jesuit posts, Munro notes, served as embassies of king and faith alike. The book is a compact English account of New France.
dave-dashaway-and-his-hydroplane-or-dari:
Roy Rockwood's Dave Dashaway and His Hydroplane is a boys' adventure novel of early aviation, subtitled Daring Adventures Over the Great Lakes. It opens at an aero meet in Columbus. A messenger boy stares in wonder at a great prize monoplane and its scarred, one-armed keeper, a veteran of endurance races against the elements.

From that airfield the story follows young aviator Dave Dashaway into flights, contests and perils over the lakes. It uses the breathless serial style that made the Rockwood name popular with boys. Machines, hangars, telegrams and races crowd the opening chapters, promising speed and danger at every turn. The book suits readers who enjoy period tales of flying, when aeroplanes were still novelties and every flight was news.
deadwood-dick-the-prince-of-the-road-or-:
A dime novel of the Black Hills fills the first number of Beadle's Half Dime Library, issued by Beadle and Adams of New York in 1877 for five cents. Edward L. Wheeler wrote it, and the hero is Deadwood Dick, prince of the road and black rider of the Black Hills.

Fearless Frank comes to the rescue in the first chapter. A wagon train of prairie schooners, midway between Cheyenne and the Black Hills, halts for a noon feed. A youth of twenty, strikingly handsome, stands out among the rough, bearded men. Ned Harris gallops up a gulch in a later scene, and faces turn deadly pale. The tale is frontier melodrama at full gallop, made for the cheap trade.
dialogue-of-comfort-against-tribulation-:
Comfort for men in trouble, in words made plain for modern readers, fills St Thomas More's dialogue in this Sheed and Ward edition of 1951. Monica Stevens did the modernizing, from the 1557 text as printed in Everyman's Library. Sheed and Ward of London and New York published it.

Stevens broke the long sentences, set the punctuation anew, and swapped dead words for live ones. Old terms too good to lose, like gigglot, were kept, and nothing was cut. Three books make the dialogue, an uncle and nephew talking through fear, loss, and death. The devil's busy tempting in times of darkness, in soul as in night, is one theme. The book is More's prison wisdom, made easy to read.
dick-prescott-s-fourth-year-at-west-poin:
The last year at West Point fills H. Irving Hancock's fourth Dick Prescott book. Its subtitle says Dick is ready to drop the gray for shoulder straps. Twenty-four chapters run from Dick reporting a brother cadet to a conclusion.

Jordan reaches out for revenge, and the class committee calls. A cadet silence falls on Dick himself: for months, as Anstey tells a small meeting, a member of the class has sat in Coventry, on barely more than a majority vote. The class takes final action as the year turns. News from Franklin Field, the Army-Navy game, and squadron drill fill the public side. A love affair and a cloud on Dick's horizon close the Academy tale.
doe-osti-17030877-development-of-fully-r:
Idaho National Laboratory report INL/RPT-26-95282, dated September 2026, describes new meshing tools for advanced reactor fuel. Katheren Bosson Nantes, Jacob Hirschhorn, Carlotta Ghezzi, and Ryan Sweet of Idaho worked with Yinbin Miao of Argonne. Their subject is TRISO fuel, tiny coated particles packed by the thousands into larger fuel forms called compacts and pebbles.

A packing algorithm places each particle center, and mesh generation then builds a fully detailed grid around every particle for the BISON fuel code. Four forms are handled: solid and hollow cylinders, and solid and hollow spheres. A worked case uses an AGR-2 test compact and maps its temperature after 300 full power days.
doe-osti-17056537-on-orbit-observations-:
Dana McGuffin of Lawrence Livermore led project 24-ERD-040, reported in October 2026, on watching stratospheric turbulence from orbit. Gravity waves rise from mountains, storms, and fronts into the stratosphere, 10 to 50 kilometers up, then break and stir the air. Small waves are hard to see, yet they push on large scale winds and climate patterns.

Data came from SOHIP, a Livermore built instrument that flew on the International Space Station from March 2023 to April 2024. It watches starlight bend and twinkle as a star sets behind the air layers. A new retrieval method reads those changes with about 3 meter vertical detail, far finer than working satellite systems give.
doe-osti-17076398-summary-of-fy-2026-lon:
Xuesong Fan and Yanli Wang of Oak Ridge National Laboratory summarize fiscal 2026 long term creep and heat aging tests on Alloy 709 in report ORNL/TM-2026/4842. Alloy 709 is a high strength steel proposed for hot parts in advanced reactors. Creep is the slow stretching of metal under load at high heat, and proving a grade for code use takes years of such tests.

A draft code case for 100,000 hour design life sits under ballot at the ASME standards body. Longer tests now running, on base metal and welds, aim at future cases for 300,000 and 500,000 hours. The longest creep exposure so far reached about 52,000 hours. Four more weld tests start in early fiscal 2027 after a lab move.
doe-osti-17076504-visualization-of-insol:
Daniel Orea and eight Oak Ridge colleagues watched how tiny particles move in molten salt in report ORNL/TM-2026/4825, dated August 2026. In a molten salt reactor, much radioactive material may travel as aerosols, fine airborne particles, made in the pump bowl or from condensed vapors. The team used a see through test cell rig called VISTA to film that behavior.

Shadow imaging, particle tracking, laser spectroscopy, and a size sorting impactor all measured one salt system at once. Tests varied gas sparging direction, sparge flow, and cover gas sweep in a lithium chloride potassium chloride salt. Nickel powder, 2.6 micrometers wide, stood in for species that do not dissolve. A first of its kind tracking run captured aerosol motion in the cover gas.
doe-osti-17197388-crada-nfe-24-10054-fin:
Bryan Maldonado and Yeonjin Bae of Oak Ridge close out CRADA NFE-24-10054 with Hearth Labs, in a final report dated September 2026. The partner's product, Q Sense, is in beta use. It builds 3D thermal point clouds of buildings, then audits their energy performance, tunes control setpoints, and guides retrofit design.

Oak Ridge contributed Auto-CuBES, short for Automatic Point Cloud Building Envelope Segmentation. The algorithm takes a point cloud from common survey gear and returns a wire frame model of the building skin. Unsupervised learning finds facades, windows, and doors with few calibration settings. Hand segmentation by a trained specialist is the slow step in retrofit panel design today. Folding the lab algorithm into the product cuts that labor sharply.
doe-osti-2583485-landscape-of-cross-lami:
Landscape study NREL/TP-5500-91113, by Swaroop Atnoorkar, Yasser El Masri, Heather Goetsch, and Chioke Harris, maps the American cross-laminated timber industry. CLT panels, layers of lumber glued crosswise, let wood build tall, and builders want them for speed and for carbon stored rather than emitted. The report asks whether U.S. supply can keep up with that demand.

Manufacturing comes first: how much is made, what timber it consumes, and where production concentrates. Barriers fill a long chapter, from press capacity and market swings to supply chains, workforce shortages, and uneven regional support. A construction chapter weighs CLT's structural advantages and cost against concrete and steel. Environmental product declarations, the labels that verify a panel's carbon claims, get their own audit of how many exist and what they cover. The landscape that emerges is of a young industry whose bottlenecks are known, named here one by one.
doe-osti-2584716-nepatec-v2-0-standardiz:
PNNL report 38163, by Sai Munikoti, Daniel Nally, Sai Koneru, and a large team, releases NEPATEC version 2.0, a standardized corpus of National Environmental Policy Act documents. NEPA reviews generate categorical exclusions, environmental assessments, and impact statements by the thousand, then scatter them across incompatible agency filing systems. The corpus gathers more than 120,000 documents from 60,000 projects and over sixty agencies into one structure.

Each document carries metadata modeled on the shared vocabulary the Council on Environmental Quality recommends, so projects, processes, and documents mean the same thing across agencies. The release aims at two audiences: officials modernizing permitting, who need the record searchable and comparable, and researchers building tools, including AI systems, over the environmental review archive. Version 2.0 expands the first release substantially. A permitting process that cannot find its own precedents repeats its own work; this corpus is the fix.
doe-osti-2586386-furthering-advancements:
Tessa Greco of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory is the technical contact on this final report, NREL/TP-5700-95553, issued in August 2025 for CRADA number CRD-19-00843. Eric Thompson shares credit for the project. The agreement supported the FAST Prize, a Department of Energy competition meant to shorten the time needed to commission pumped storage hydropower plants.

The report is a plain closeout filing, and it reads like one. Greco coordinated the project's deliverables, which included a public abstract when the agreement was signed and a technical volume presenting the prize work. A presentation prepared for the competition's Pitch Day is also listed among the products. The filing records that the project produced no subject inventions and no registered reports of invention. It exists to satisfy the final report clause of the agreement.
doe-osti-2586532-furthering-advancements:
Tessa Greco of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory is the technical contact on this final report, NREL/TP-5700-95650, issued in August 2025 for CRADA number CRD-19-00836. David Gatto shares credit for the project. The agreement supported finalists in the FAST Prize, a Department of Energy competition meant to shorten the time needed to commission pumped storage hydropower plants.

The intent of the project was to support Team Gatto and Ames Construction, one of the prize finalist teams. The filing records the deliverables Greco coordinated: a public abstract at the start of the agreement, a technical volume presenting the work, and a presentation prepared for the competition's Pitch Day. Business advisement for the finalists is also noted. Like the other filings in this series, it closes by recording that the project produced no subject inventions.
doe-osti-2587163-electrocatalytically-up:
Jianhua Tong of Clemson University led this project under cooperative agreement DE-FE0031871, running from June 2020 through May 2025, with the final report submitted on August 31, 2025. Kyle Brinkman, Fei Peng, and Hai Xiao at Clemson, plus Zili Wu at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, served as co-investigators. Total funding was 1.25 million dollars. The goal was to upgrade methane, the main part of natural gas, into benzene, a far more valuable chemical building block.

The team built a highly compacted microchannel reactor around a protonic ceramic membrane. In such a cell, an electric field pulls hydrogen away as methane reacts, pushing the chemistry toward aromatics. Test chapters follow single cells through fuel cell mode runs, including a stability run drawing 200 milliamps per square centimeter at 650 degrees Celsius. Additive manufacturing features in the reactor build, matching the project's keywords.
doe-osti-2589617-tritium-containment-ves:
Randy Shurtz, Alvaro Cruz-Cabrera, Carl Fitzgerald, and Lynelle Takahashi test how tritium containment vessels behave under fire and impact abuse, in Sandia report SAND2025-11734. Tritium is a radioactive form of hydrogen used in weapons and fusion work. Safety reviews must show its containers will not leak badly in accidents.

Test hardware was heated, dropped, and watched with cameras, including an infrared camera at a marked drop zone inside a safety cage. Valve leakage was a special focus, with two test series run as temperatures climbed. Gas sampling lines fed a residual gas analyzer during the abuse runs. Results feed fire safety assessments that set storage and transport rules for tritium systems.
doe-osti-2997462-investigation-of-reacti:
University of Notre Dame final report on award DE-SC0025543, led by David Go, studies how methane behaves inside a dielectric barrier discharge plasma. Work ran at the Princeton Collaborative Research Facility under the Fusion Energy Sciences program. Barrier discharges drive chemistry without heating the whole gas, a route toward converting light hydrocarbons with electricity.

Dense, overlapping spectra blocked the usual curve-fitting route to molecule counts: acetylene and ethylene signals blur together. The team built a MATLAB spectrum analyzer that fits each species on its clean spectral stretches first, then rebuilds the blended regions from those pieces. Temperature effects that suppress the chemistry are the second thread in the title. Plasma chemists get both a measurement fix and reaction pathway data for methane conversion studies.
doe-osti-2997603-slug-test-characterizat:
Savannah River National Laboratory report SRNL-STI-2025-00305, by Kenneth Dixon, dated September 2025, reports quick water tests in 21 wells at the Chemicals, Metals, and Pesticides Pits cleanup area. The wells tap the Upper Three Runs aquifer, the water table aquifer at the site, which has three stacked zones split by two leaky confining layers. Knowing each zone's hydraulic traits feeds the groundwater model used to track contamination.

Each slug test dropped or pulled a solid PVC rod of known volume in the well and logged the water level's recovery with a pressure sensor. Both falling-head and rising-head runs were done per well. Zones covered are the shallow transmissive zone, the middle aquifer zone, and the lower aquifer zone, which reaches down to the green clay confining layer. The data set updates flow and transport modeling for the pits area.
doe-osti-2997611-ascorbic-acid-stability:
Holly VerMeulen, Evan Koelker, and Sophia Fuentes test vitamin C as a treatment chemical for contaminated well water, in Savannah River report SRNL-STI-2025-00578 dated September 2025. A pilot wellhead system, RWM-018, would dose pumped groundwater with ascorbic acid to neutralize oxidant pollution. Feasibility hinges on how fast the acid breaks down and how it shifts water acidity across the treatment network.

Stability trials exposed the acid to light and to heat, then checked how much reducing power remained. Efficacy scoping used a probe watching oxidation-reduction potential in real time; neutralization counted as complete when the reading fell fast and leveled off low. One scoping run sized the dose for 140 milliliters of solution carrying 1,500 parts per billion of oxidant, using a 2 molar acid stock. Results feed the go or no-go call on the pilot.
doe-osti-2997985-remote-sensing-approach:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report, by Kyle Larson, Victoria Sinnott, and Andre Coleman, dated September 2025, tests watching tree health from satellites along power line corridors. Trees that sicken and fall cause outages and spark fires, but walking every mile of corridor is slow. The method tracks a greenness index, NDVI, which rises and falls with plant productivity, and looks for drops over time.

Change metrics were checked against the federal LANDFIRE disturbance maps, 2023 release, which log wildfire, insect and disease damage, cutting, and windthrow with the year each happened. Forest patches with mapped disturbances were compared against quiet patches to test how sharply the greenness signal reacts. Areas of concern were then flagged for closer review. Utilities gain a screening layer that points ground crews at the spans most worth visiting.
doe-osti-3000283-initial-uncertainty-ana:
Xiaoliang He, Mark Rockhold and Xuehang Song of Pacific Northwest open an uncertainty study in PNNL-38406, dated September 2025, on a stubborn Hanford pollutant. Carbon tetrachloride, once used in plutonium work, lingers under the site's Central Plateau in the Ringold A and Lower Mud rock units. Cleanup planning needs forecasts of where the plume will go and how long it will last. Honest ranges matter more than single lines on a map.

A large Monte Carlo study ran the Plateau to River model many times over. Three unknowns were varied. The contaminant's decay rate came first, with half-lives from 70 to 700 years. The starting plume shape was drawn as 100 plausible versions. Water flow speed through each rock unit also got 100 versions apiece. The initial results map how those unknowns spread the forecast, giving remediation planners a defensible sense of what is known and what is not.
doe-osti-3002152-multimodal-atomic-force:
Jennifer Neu, Avery Wood, Duncan Moseley, Chad Parish, Andrew Miskowiec, and Zach Brubaker report a microscopy study in Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/4168, dated October 2025. Their tool is the atomic force microscope, which feels a surface with a fine tip instead of using light. Running it in several modes at once gives shape plus other traits, such as stiffness or magnetism, in one scan. The samples are tiny metallic particles.

The team tested the method on varied particle sets. It mapped surface shape and functional traits without destroying the samples. Results on mixed materials, from silver to iron oxide particles, showed limits in scaling the technique across unlike samples. The authors call for in-place standards to make readings more repeatable. Forensics and materials labs are the audience.
doe-osti-3003002-past-approaches-for-spe:
Rob P. Rechard, Hank Jenkins-Smith, and Kuhika Gupta write part two of a waste disposal history in Sandia report SAND2025-13801, printed October 2025. Where part one covered safety standards, this volume covers people and process: how repository sites were chosen, how development was staged, and what the public actually preferred. The wastes are the same: spent fuel, high-level waste, and transuranic waste.

Chapters trace United States policy from the commitment to geologic disposal in the Nuclear Waste Policy Act through its halting implementation. The Environmental Protection Agency standard at the Waste Isolation Pilot Plant appears as the one working example. Jenkins-Smith brings survey research on public preferences to the record. The volume speaks to policymakers designing a consent-based siting process today, armed with what earlier rounds taught.
doe-osti-3004456-materials-for-energy-ma:
Anna Hiszpanski of Lawrence Livermore gives an abbreviated final report for LDRD project 23-ERD-049, LLNL-TR-2013336, dated November 2025. The project, called MEMES, developed materials that manage energy across the electromagnetic spectrum: surfaces and films that steer, absorb, or emit light and heat by design. Electrification is one driver, since buildings, vehicles, and devices all leak energy as light and heat.

Work included electrophoretic displays that use structural color rather than pigments, needing power mainly when the image changes. Particle behavior in iron oxide and silica nanoparticle displays was studied across conference papers. One patent application covers products using vertically aligned carbon nanotubes to modulate light transmission. Abbreviated LDRD reports are short by design: they record the project's aims, outputs, and intellectual property for the laboratory's portfolio.
doe-osti-3005209-doe-as-a-digital-innova:
Michael Sparrow files a short final report for DOE grant DE-SC0024261, which made the department a digital innovation sponsor of the WCRP Open Science Conference 2023. The World Climate Research Programme's once-in-a-decade meeting ran October 23 to 27, 2023, in Kigali, Rwanda. More than 1,500 people took part in person and online.

The report records what the sponsorship supported, including learning labs and a two-day symposium for early and mid-career researchers hosted by the African Institute for Mathematical Sciences. The conference connected to Energy Department programs in atmospheric system research and earth system modeling. Its outputs include the Kigali Declaration and a set of media and reflection pieces. Sponsor reports like this one are brief by design: they account for the grant against the event it underwrote.
doe-osti-3006477-studying-open-quantum-s:
Final report dated November 28, 2025, from UC Berkeley closes award DE-SC0023277, a $570,000 project led by Hartmut Haeffner with Birgitta Whaley as partner. The work advanced a trapped-ion quantum simulator as a platform for open quantum systems, the kind met in chemistry and light harvesting. The ions' vibrational motion is the key resource. It can be manipulated and measured precisely, coupled to auxiliary qubits, and used as a sensitive quantum sensor or as a programmable environment bath.

Three outcomes headline the summary. The vibrational mode served as an ultrasensitive probe for tests of fundamental physics, including possible nonlinear quantum mechanics effects. The modes also acted as controllable baths, where tuned noise and loss changed energy-transfer dynamics. A third line introduced controllable nonlinear gain and loss. The lessons section says obstacles slowed parts of the plan but left stronger infrastructure and clearer directions.
doe-osti-3007893-ray-tracing-simulations:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/TM-2025/4121, dated September 2025, uses ray-tracing simulations to rate a proposed new main shutter. Its authors are Matthew Frost, Garrett Granroth, and Thomas Huegle. The shutter serves the HB4 beamline at the High Flux Isotope Reactor and is planned for 2028.

The shutter carries guide channels that steer cold neutrons to instruments, and channel shape and reflectivity get their own design section. The study works through the cold source and beamtube, then scores the design across the 1.0 to 4.5 angstrom wavelength band. Alignment studies tilt the shutter through small yaw angles to measure how fast performance degrades. The results set the tolerances the real shutter must be built and installed to.
doe-osti-3013462-fy25-theory-and-simulat:
Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2024/3520, dated August 2024, documents a fusion theory and simulation performance target: an integrated modeling framework for reactor design and assessment. The hosted text carries that report number and an author line led by P. Humrickhouse, with J. Lore, J. M. Park, and co-authors. It argues that fusion pilot plants will operate beyond today's experience, so design, safety, and cost calls must lean on physics-based simulation.

The framework couples whole-device models with edge plasma codes. One benchmark ran the same case in SOLPS-ITER and BOUT++/Hermes-3 with 100 megawatts crossing the core boundary, half to electrons and half to ions. Photon fluxes agreed in shape, while the BOUT++ radiation came out significantly lower. Such cross-checks show where integrated predictions can be trusted for pilot plant decisions.
doe-osti-3019939-evaluation-of-technolog:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/SPR-2025/4162, by Alexander Johs and six co-authors, evaluates materials that trap elemental mercury vapor inside waste disposal containers. Demolition work at the Y-12 National Security Complex produces mercury-contaminated debris. During storage and transport, temperature swings can turn mercury vapor into liquid droplets, and disposal sites forbid free liquids in solid waste containers.

In small laboratory tests, the team measured how well sorbent materials suppressed mercury vapor above liquid mercury over periods up to 973 hours. They also tested how heat and moisture changed performance across a 14-day experiment. Some sorbents lost much of their effect at higher temperatures. Vermiculite performed no better than the control with no sorbent at all. The findings point to which materials can keep mercury vapor locked down until disposal.
doe-osti-3020532-numerical-modeling-amp-:
NLR CRADA final report NLR/TP-5700-95767, CRD-24-29969, by Salman Husain, continues joint work with iProTech on its Pitching Inertial Pump wave energy converter. The device pitches with ocean waves and pumps water through a hydraulic circuit to generate power. Earlier work mapped the design space; this TEAMER project refined the computer model and tested control strategies in the WEC-Sim simulation software.

Model upgrades added Coulomb friction, a controllable bypass valve, and motorized valves in place of passive check valves. The team then compared control methods from simple latching control to reinforcement learning, aiming for strong performance across ocean conditions. The modeling exposed numerical sensitivities in the hydraulic circuit, where accumulator pressures differed from coil pressures by orders of magnitude. iProTech updated its 3D designs alongside the simulation work.
doe-osti-3020547-generator-interconnecti:
LBNL slide deck by Joachim Seel, Nick Manderlink, Julie Mulvaney Kemp, and co-authors, dated February 2026. It presents research on what it costs power generators to connect to the grid outside the big regional markets. Before a project can be built, grid operators study it and assign the cost of needed network upgrades. High assigned costs often push developers to withdraw, clogging the interconnection queue.

The cost sample covers five non-ISO balancing authorities, including PacifiCorp, the Bonneville Power Administration, and Duke's territories. It represents 55 percent of recent generators and storage that requested interconnection there from 2020 to 2024. Costs are broken down by queue status, fuel type, project size, and location. Many completed projects had low costs, while a minority faced very high ones. The deck points readers to the underlying public dataset.
doe-osti-3021629-community-scale-solar-p:
Forest County Potawatomi Community final technical report for DOE award DE-IE0000120, by project manager Sara M. Drescher, dated February 19, 2026, reports community-scale solar installations across tribal facilities in Wisconsin. Total project costs were $2,155,758, with DOE's Office of Indian Energy providing $1,724,606. The Tribe's long-term goal is energy independence, guided by Potawatomi values of taking from the earth only what is needed.

Solar systems went onto or beside ten tribally owned facilities, together producing over one megawatt and saving an estimated $107,000 a year. The work took two rounds: seven sites installed by the original contractor in 2022, then three more in 2024 after land use changes forced new site choices. Months of follow-up fixed construction issues and repaired ice storm damage, and remote monitoring was added at the sites.
doe-osti-3022821-preliminary-seismic-yie:
LLNL report LLNL-TR-2008467, by Arthur Rodgers, Taka'aki Taira, and Sean Ford, estimates the explosive yield of the July 1, 2025 explosions near Esparto, California, from seismic recordings. The blasts, at a fireworks storage site, were recorded regionally, and seismologists can invert those signals for source size, information the authors note may inform forensic analysis of the disaster.

The analysis is careful about what the waves carry. Air blast dominated the full waveforms. It traveled near the speed of sound, about 350 meters per second at the day's 36 degree temperature. Seismic P waves moved near 4,100 meters per second and were weak by comparison. Filtering to the seismic arrivals and applying a scaled-source model gives yields across the events in the range of 1,500 to 4,700 kilograms of TNT equivalent.
doe-osti-3023693-enabling-solar-cybersec:
Kirsten Verclas of the National Association of State Energy Officials led this final report for award DE-EE0009004, which ran from March 2020 to February 2025, signed July 7, 2025. Campbell Delahoyde and Sarah Trent are also named. The project worked through state energy offices and public utility commissions, with private partners, to get solar cybersecurity solutions adopted rather than merely published.

Through expert presentations and peer exchanges, states picked out strategies for folding solar cybersecurity planning into formal state plans, policies, and procedures, including State Energy Security Plans. A closing task built a strategy and final memo for integrating the solar cybersecurity advisory group into NASEO and NARUC programming, so the work would live inside standing state energy networks.
doe-osti-3024011-plasma-surface-interact:
Davide Curreli of the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign led award DE-SC0018141, which ran from September 2017 to August 2024, on plasma-facing components in magnetic fusion machines. The Illinois team's full name for the problem is in the title: predicting how dynamic wall surfaces perform and what they do to the plasma. Tungsten walls erode, reflect fuel, and trap tritium, and each process feeds back on the others.

The project built and linked high-performance simulation tools for sputtering, dynamic recycling of fuel species, and tritium implantation and retention. A model of the magnetic presheath, the thin layer where plasma meets wall, got an early experimental check using three-dimensional laser-induced fluorescence data from the HELIX device at West Virginia University. Published results include a 2024 Nuclear Fusion paper on dynamic recycling in divertors.
doe-osti-3024042-a-framework-for-buildin:
Stephen Reed, Scott Nelson, Michael Sharp, and Alyson Coates of Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Steven Horowitz and Emily Sandt of Sandia, and Chris Chwasz and Shannon Eggers of Idaho National Laboratory. Together they wrote this framework in January 2026 for the Office of International Nuclear Security. Its premise is in the title: security works best when built into a facility's design process early, not bolted on after drawings harden.

The document is organized as chapters a design team can work through, and its reference tables run deep into classic nuclear siting topics. Listings cover hydrologic descriptions, floods and probable maximum flood, potential dam failures, seismic classification, and stability of subsurface materials and foundations. Protection against piping failures in fluid systems outside containment also appears. The framework ties those engineering checks to security decisions.
doe-osti-3027552-geothermal-direct-use-a:
Abra Gold, Amy Allen, Hannah Pauling, Shanti Pless, and Mara Koerner of the National Laboratory of the Rockies studied geothermal heat for Bucharest's district energy system in report NLR/TP-5700-93613, dated March 2026. District systems move hot water from a central plant to whole neighborhoods, and Bucharest's is extensive but lossy. Using the earth's heat directly, without first making electricity, is the proposition tested here.

In the modeled layout, a heat pump at the end-use site lifts geothermal water to space heating and hot water temperatures. Distribution losses decide much of the case. Modelica modeling put total heat loss at 10 to 20 percent if old district pipes are replaced with insulated ones. A more cautious GEOPHIRES scenario kept today's network, where a 40 percent heat loss figure, shared on a field visit, was expected.
doe-osti-3029149-collider-physics-instru:
Sally Seidel of the University of New Mexico reports collider physics instrumentation work in a final report dated March 18, 2026. Engineers Martin Hoeferkamp and Jiahe Si worked with her, along with a bench of graduate and honors students. Six goals organize the program, all circling one problem: silicon detectors at colliders must keep timing and collecting charge after years of radiation damage.

The team developed thin three-dimensional silicon sensors that multiply charge before and after irradiation, characterized DC-LGAD designs including carbon implantation and tighter electrode spacing. They pushed AC-LGADs toward full fill factor. On the analysis side, ATLAS pixel leakage current from Runs 1 and 2 calibrates simulations of future detector lifetime, with Hamburg model variants tested against dedicated high-voltage scan runs. Irradiation access ran through a Sandia CRADA renewed in 2024 for sixty more months.
doe-osti-3030348-a-framework-for-buildin:
Stephen Reed, Scott Nelson, and Michael Sharp of Oak Ridge National Laboratory, with Sandia and Idaho lab co-authors, offer design guidance dated January 2026 from the Office of International Nuclear Security. Their theme is security by design: build protection into a nuclear facility from the first sketches, not bolt it on later. The advice targets design vendors and plant operators. It works through a firm quality management system, the paperwork trail firms already use to prove their work is sound.

Chapters walk through how security goals should shape siting, layout, and system choices. Reference lists cover hazards from floods and earthquakes to wind, tornadoes, and pipe breaks, since guards and barriers must survive the same events as the plant. The aim is a facility where safety and security reinforce each other instead of competing.
doe-osti-3362562-application-of-electroc:
Guoping Cao, Guy L. Fredrickson, and Ken C. Marsden of Idaho National Laboratory review salt monitoring in technical letter report TLR-RES/DE/REB-2025-04, dated April 2025. The Nuclear Regulatory Commission is building the know-how to license molten salt reactors. In such a reactor the salt chemistry must stay in a set range, since its oxidation state, called RedOx, drives how fast the salt corrodes the vessel and pipes. The report judges whether electric sensing can watch that state live.

Two electric methods lead: potentiometry, which reads the resting voltage between a sensor and a reference electrode, and voltammetry, which sweeps voltage and watches current. Both have long use in salt chemistry studies. The review also maps salt types, from fuel-bearing fast reactor salts to solid fuel cooled by clean salt, since each narrows the sensor choices.
doe-osti-3363510-zero-order-reactioin-ki:
Russell Whitesides of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory and Syed Wahiduzzaman of Gamma Technologies close out CRADA TC02369 in this May 2026 final report (LLNL-TR-2015675). The project brought the laboratory's Zero-RK chemical kinetics software into Gamma's GT-SUITE engine simulation package, so detailed chemistry could run inside practical combustion models. Technical work ended in June 2023.

Benchmarks show the payoff. On a zero dimensional case with a 47 species mechanism, run time fell from 320 seconds to 170 seconds with negligible change in peak pressure, power, or burn rates. With 198 species, run time dropped from over 150 minutes to 32 minutes, roughly a fivefold speedup that makes emissions grade chemistry affordable in routine simulations.
doe-osti-3364119-startr-an-open-source-m:
An Idaho National Laboratory poster, INL/EXP-25-86587, by Daniel Everett Grammer with mentors Travis Louis Lange and Thomas Folk, dates to August 2025. It presents STARTR, an open-source model of a MARVEL-class microreactor built for the National Reactor Innovation Center's Virtual Test Bed. The model runs in OpenMC, a neutron transport code, and describes a sodium-cooled, thermal-spectrum test reactor.

The fuel meat is uranium-zirconium hydride, which also moderates neutrons and gives the core a safety-friendly negative temperature coefficient. Heating from cold zero power to hot full power hardens the neutron spectrum, and heating the beryllium reflectors hardened it more in isolated tests. Power peaking factors, mapped radially and axially, flatten at full power as control drums withdraw. The poster shares the model so industry and university users can practice microreactor physics.
doe-osti-3374756-participation-in-and-as:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/TM-2026/4618, dated June 2026, records the lab's part in the third DNCSH public workshop. Five authors are named: Walid Metwally, Don Algama, and Lindsey Aloisi head the list. Andrew Barto and William Wieselquist complete it. The workshop series is run by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission. Its work ties to criticality safety for high-assay low-enriched uranium, a fuel class new reactors will need.

Earlier workshops met in February 2024 and August 2025. The report describes what Oak Ridge brought to the third session and weighs how the session went. Background items include a Department of Energy award of seventeen million dollars, made in October 2025. That money funds the first round of HALEU criticality benchmarking work. Benchmark data of that kind underpins the safety cases the workshops discuss.
doe-osti-3376603-growth-and-research-opp:
A final technical report for the GROWTH-MSI program covers a traineeship that opens particle physics to students at minority serving schools. Wing To of CSU Stanislaus and Alexandra Miller of Sonoma State University led it. The award, DE-SC0023876, sits in the Energy Department's RENEW push. Six Northern California campuses took part, from San Francisco State to UC Merced. Their students often lack local particle physics courses, faculty, and funds. The program set out to clear each of those blocks at once.

The traineeship runs a year and a half. It pays students for research time and pairs them with local and outside mentors. A new Introduction to Particle Physics course anchors the study side. At Sonoma State it was built as an online course, with taped lectures and exams. It won curriculum approval, so it can outlive the grant. Weekly seminars brought lab research to all six campuses.
doe-osti-3388178-develop-renewable-susta:
Develop Renewable/Sustainable Material to Displace Petroleum-Derived Polymer Foams is the charge written into CRADA final report NLR/TP-2800-100346, dated July 2026, under agreement CRD-22-22955. Peter Ciesielski is the National Laboratory of the Rockies technical contact and cited author. Funding came from the Bioenergy Technologies Office.

Polymer foams cushion packages, insulate buildings, and pad furniture, and nearly all of them start as petroleum. A renewable replacement has to match the foam's lightness and spring at a price factories can pay, or it displaces nothing. The cooperative project developed candidate materials toward that bar, drawing on the laboratory's biomass materials work. The final report closes the agreement with the partners' cleared summary of what was made and learned.
doe-osti-3409786-digital-twin-visualizin:
Kenny Gruchalla of the National Laboratory of the Rockies gave a Grid Talk slide deck on digital twins for the power grid, dated May 28, 2026. A digital twin is a live model that mirrors a real system. The talk starts with a classic warning about blind trust in summary numbers.

Slides use Anscombe's Quartet to show that matching averages can hide very different data. Past lab work pictured voltage control with high solar shares and a net-zero district display. The point for grid staff: good pictures of data help people think, not just compute. Twins must aid judgment, not replace it.
doe-osti-3430773-development-and-impleme:
CRADA final report dated August 17, 2026 covers high-throughput proteomic and metabolomics assays using advanced chromatography and mass spectrometry. Parties included Agilent Technologies, Sandia, Battelle at Pacific Northwest, and Berkeley Lab. Christopher Petzold was the Berkeley Lab contact.

Runs on one platform covered several microbes, with dates in August 2020. Aspergillus niger alone accounted for 64 runs in the table shown. Two collision energy settings were used across the runs. Shared methods let labs compare protein and metabolite data across sites. Faster assays speed strain screening for bioenergy research work. Skyline software handled mass spectrometry data in the shared workflow studies described.
doe-osti-3453387-modelling-external-tran:
Sandia report SAND2026-25231R, by Maxwell Zengel with Martin Rieth, builds an OpenFOAM workflow for air flow around a Boeing 737-like aircraft at cruise. The work targets contrails, the ice clouds from aircraft exhaust. Contrail cirrus may drive about 30 percent of aviation's warming effect, the abstract states, citing past work.

Solver settings balanced stability against run time over thousands of steps. Extra corrector steps cost hours, so the final settings compromise. Boundary choices also shaped stability and realism. Wing tip vortices tangle with exhaust plumes in these runs. Climate modelers gain a base flow for longer contrail studies.
ebooks-neither-e-nor-books-paper-for-the:
Cory Doctorow argues that ebooks are neither e nor books in a paper for the O'Reilly Emerging Technologies Conference, given at San Diego on February 12, 2004. He gave the text itself to the public domain, and notes with a grin that the slides cannot be shared for copyright reasons. The talk grew out of his own novel, Down and Out in the Magic Kingdom, released free online.

Doctorow attacks the fears of publishers one by one. Book-rippers who corrupt texts for sport, he says, are a phantom; he has never seen evidence that any exist. Cheap copying, he argues, helps unknown writers far more than it hurts them, since obscurity is the true enemy. The paper is a brisk, funny brief for open sharing, written when ebooks were still a fight about the future. It stands as a period piece of the early web's copyright wars.
from-london-to-land-s-end-and-two-letter:
Daniel Defoe's From London to Land's End, printed by Cassell in 1888, collects letters from his Tour through the whole island of Great Britain. The introduction warns that two letters from another gentleman's similar Journey are appended, and that mixed sets often confuse purchasers. Defoe's own letters march west through southern England.

He describes towns, trade, ruins, and curiosities with a journalist's appetite: Portland nearly an island, its beach joining the shore, and Abbotsbury famous now only for its abbey ruins. Defoe traveled as a government agent and merchant as much as an author. His Tour remains a prime source for England's economy and landscape in the 1720s, brisk and opinionated on every page.
govdocs-archive_org-MasonicTempleToPadre:
A special edition of the Italian Catholic journal Chiesa viva, number 381 of March 2006, asks whether the new church of St. Padre Pio is in fact a Masonic temple. Franco Adessa, with Father Luigi Villa, presents the case. The church at San Giovanni Rotondo, Padre Pio's town, had opened in 2004 to designs by Renzo Piano.

The authors read the building's forms, numbers, and symbols as Masonic signs hidden in a Catholic shrine. Theirs is a traditionalist polemic, richly illustrated and wholly convinced. The edition is held as it appeared: an artifact of the quarrels over modern church design and the memory of Italy's most loved modern saint.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIADowneyJohnT_:
John T. Downey was a CIA officer whose plane was shot down over China in 1952, on a mission connected with an agent extraction. Captured and sentenced to life, he spent twenty years in Chinese prisons. This Washington Post article by Thomas O'Toole, dated March 18, 1973, meets him coming home.

Downey's release came with the Nixon opening to China, and he walked out the longest-held prisoner of the CIA's early Cold War. O'Toole tells the capture, the decades in which Washington denied he was an intelligence officer, and the return. The article is the homecoming chapter of a famous spy case.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MarksSidTheWatl:
Sid Marks told the FBI a short story from November 23, 1963, the day after the assassination. He was in the offices of detective Dick Hathcock when Hathcock's associate, Roy Payne, came in. Payne asked whether anyone had been in to get a rifle. The bureau wrote the account up as a report, filed as LA 89-75 and known here as the Watley Report.

Reports like this one fill the assassination files by the thousand. Each preserves a single odd remark or errand that might matter. A question about a rifle, asked the day after the shooting, was exactly the kind of detail agents were told to record. The report keeps the wording, the office, and the date.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-NelsonJohnT_Nel:
Harold Weisberg wrote to John T. Nelson of New Orleans on November 23, 1970. A Times-Picayune story had quoted Weisberg, and the letter takes that story as its starting point. Weisberg also describes his own independent investigations of political assassinations in New Orleans.

New Orleans was the second front of assassination research, home to the Garrison inquiry and to many Oswald leads. Weisberg worked the city by correspondence, correcting newspapers and trading findings with local contacts. The letter to Nelson shows that work at desk level: a clipping received, a reply drafted, a claim about his investigations restated for the record. It also dates his New Orleans inquiries to at least 1970.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-NoguchiThomasT_: Thomas TNoguchi - the coroner to the stars - lends his name to this declassified US government file at the Internet Archive. No date, no office, no description rides along with the title. The text itself has not surfaced. A named shell, kept for completeness.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-TranscriptsWash: On May 19, 1974, the Washington Post printed another White House tape transcript, the sixth in its series. Newspapers across the country raced to publish the Nixon tapes as they were released that spring. Each transcript let readers judge the president's private words for themselves. The Post's series forms a day-by-day public record of Watergate as it broke open in print.
govdocs-archive_org-the-esoteric-hitleri: The Esoteric Hitlerism of Jason Alfred Thompkins 3rd: the volume - the made public government document, subject: government records. Held as an archive item; no stance taken, a single volume, dated entry. From the archive shelves, for readers.
govdocs-archive_org-theoretical-biophysi: Dakota Frandsen published a 2026 study of an alleged 1993 incident involving Soviet soldiers. Its long title uses dense terms from physics and earth science. The library holds the work as an archive item, without backing, and classes it as fringe material. Its technical style dresses a strange claim in the forms of hard science. It serves readers who study how fringe claims present themselves to the world.
govdocs-archive_org-understanding-realit:
Chang Po-tuan, a Song-dynasty master, wrote Understanding Reality in the eleventh century as a classic of Taoist internal alchemy. The text is presented here with commentary.

Internal alchemy treats the body itself as the furnace: breath, essence, and spirit are refined into an inner elixir, the Tao made real in a person. Chang's verses are dense and coded, which is why commentary travels with them. The work is a cornerstone of Taoist literature. Readers of Chinese religion meet in it one of the tradition's most studied guides to the inner path.
history-of-the-conquest-of-peru-with-a-p:
William Hickling Prescott's Conquest of Peru appears in this fuller version with its footnotes and a preliminary view of the civilization of the Incas, as its companion headnote explains. The preface again describes the nearly blind historian's apparatus: notes in hieroglyphic characters, a blind man's writing-case, and a secretary grown expert at reading both. The same Claudian and Lope de Vega mottoes open the work.

The preliminary view surveys Inca government, religion, agriculture, and arts before Pizarro lands. Churches built of ancient stones, altars raised where the sun's image shone, show the conquest's layering in the middle books. With notes intact, this edition serves readers who want Prescott's evidence as well as his narrative.
home-vegetable-gardening-a-complete-and-:
F. F. Rockwell's Home Vegetable Gardening is a complete and practical guide to planting and caring for vegetables, fruits and berries worth growing at home. Rockwell writes as first aid for gardeners whose experience is narrow and whose spare time is limited.

High prices make the home garden a great help, Rockwell notes, as well as a hobby, and his aim is practical, efficient gardening with the least fuss and loss of time. Garden books, he observes, seldom lack information but often fail to present it clearly. His volume tries to be comprehensive yet simple and concise. Home gardeners will find it a sensible, old-fashioned manual that still earns its place.
in-the-heart-of-the-vosges-and-other-ske:
Matilda Betham-Edwards, who called herself a devious traveller, wrote sketches of unfrequented France in this 1911 book. Some pieces were new, others reprinted from an out-of-print work. She thanks Maurice Barres and Andre Hallays for views of Alsace. Montaigne's line on travel heads the book.

The Vosges and Alsace supply villages, art, and local life. A long passage weighs why some great works fail despite their makers' faith. Doré's early work is among the art discussed. Betham-Edwards writes as an English traveller who knew France deeply and sought its byways.
journals-of-travels-in-assam-burma-bhoot:
William Griffith's Journals of Travels record journeys in Assam, Burma, Bhootan, Afghanistan, and nearby countries. John M'Clelland arranged the journals for publication, in an edition from 1847. The contents open with a notice of Griffith's life from the Linnaean Society. His first journey went with the Assam deputation examining the tea plant.

Later chapters cross the Mishmee mountains and the tea districts of Upper Assam. Griffith traveled toward Hookum and on to Ava, noting plants as he went. He descended the Irrawaddi to Rangoon and journeyed into Bootan with notes on plant distribution. As a botanist, Griffith filled his travel diary with the plants of each region. The journals mix mission travel, science, and close natural observation.
lecture-on-the-aborigines-of-newfoundlan:
Joseph Noad delivered this lecture on the aborigines of Newfoundland in January 1859. He spoke before the Mechanics' Institute at St. John's. Noad served as surveyor-general of the colony.

R. J. Parsons printed the lecture at St. John's that year. Noad surveys rival theories about the island's first people. His office gave him wide knowledge of Newfoundland's coasts and interior. The Beothuk and other peoples stand behind his inquiry. The lecture preserves early colonial thinking about Indigenous history, with its limits. Mechanics' institutes brought lectures to working audiences then. Noad's talk joined local pride to early anthropology.
legends-of-the-middle-ages-narrated-with:
H. A. Guerber narrated Legends of the Middle Ages in 1896. Her subtitle stresses links with literature and art. She dedicated the book to her sister Adele.

Old lines about Arthur and Charlemagne open her preface. Roland's fights with Saracens stand among her chosen tales. Guerber built the book for students meeting medieval romance. Clear retelling matters more to her than scholarly dispute. Teachers used her legends to lead young readers toward the great originals. Siegfried, Beowulf, and the Nibelungs enter her survey too. Art works named in the text guide museum visits.
life-letters-and-epicurean-philosophy-of:
Ninon de l'Enclos, famed beauty of seventeenth-century France, fills this 1903 volume. Robinson and Overton published the life, letters, and philosophy together. Early chapters weigh Ninon as a standard and as a parallel. Her youth and the morals of her period follow.

Count de Coligny enters the story of her early attachments. The Birds of the Tournelles nickname her circle of admirers. Her mother's death marks a turning point in the narrative. The letters let readers judge her celebrated wit for themselves. Her mother's death changes the household's course in the biography. Later chapters follow Ninon's salon fame and her written philosophy.
michael-angelo-buonarroti-with-translati:
Charles Holroyd, keeper of the National Gallery of British Art, published this study of Michelangelo in 1903. Alongside his own account, Holroyd prints translations of two early sources. The first is the life of the master written by his pupil Ascanio Condivi. The second is three dialogues from the Portuguese of Francisco d'Ollanda.

Plates reproduce the David, the Moses, the Pietà, and scenes from the Sistine ceiling. Readers can thus compare the Renaissance testimony with the works themselves. Condivi knew Michelangelo personally, so his biography carries unusual weight. The volume serves students who want both the art and the earliest written record of its maker.
morien-a-metrical-romance-rendered-into-:
Jessie L. Weston rendered this Arthurian romance into English prose from the medieval Dutch. It is number four in her Arthurian Romances series. Her preface explains the source: a metrical romance inside the Dutch version of the Lancelot. There it runs past five thousand lines, closing the compilation's first volume.

So far as anyone knows, the romance survives nowhere else. Neither its date nor its author is known; the manuscript is early fourteenth century. Morien is a Moorish knight who comes to Arthur's court seeking his father. Weston, a leading Arthurian scholar, compared such compilations to Malory's, and her translation rescued a unique tale.
mountain-pictures-and-other-poems-part-2:
John Greenleaf Whittier's poems of nature fill this part of his collected works. The Mountain Pictures sequence opens the selection. Its two parts view Franconia from the Pemigewasset and Monadnock from Wachuset. Whittier hails the mountains of the North, asking them to unveil their brows once more.

Other poems include The Vanishers, The Pressed Gentian, and Sunset on the Bearcamp. The Trailing Arbutus, Storm on Lake Asquam, and A Summer Pilgrimage follow. Whittier, the Quaker poet of New England, mixes exact local scenery with religious feeling. These nature poems sit beside subjective and religious pieces in the same gathered volume.
narrative-of-a-voyage-to-the-northwest-c:
Gabriel Franchere tells of the first American settlement on the Pacific. His voyage covered 1811 through 1814 on the Northwest Coast. J. V. Huntington translated and edited the book. Redfield issued it in New York in 1854.

A picture shows Astoria as it stood in 1813. Senator Thomas Benton quoted the book in an 1846 Senate speech. He called it the fullest, most trusted source on Oregon's claims. Franchere, a British subject on the Columbia, wrote without slant, Benton said. The tale covers the Tonquin, the post's founding, and its fall in war, by an eyewitness clerk.
nasa-tm-19650020356-auroral-particles-fr:
T W Speiser at Goddard wrote this first paper on where auroral particles come from. The aurora is lit by charged particles striking the upper air. Many are thought to arrive from the geomagnetic tail, the long part of Earth's magnetic field blown away from the Sun. Speiser follows particle paths near a neutral sheet in that tail.

Field models are used to predict how the particles behave. Their paths decide where they enter the air and light the sky. The paper is marked part one, so a series was planned. It reflects early work on a question that satellite data were only beginning to answer.
nasa-tm-19660021056-fin-a-computer-progr:
FIN is the name of a computer program described in this April 1966 Goddard report, numbered X-721-66-162. The program calculates the aerodynamic characteristics of fins at supersonic speeds. Fins guide rockets and missiles, and their lift and drag must be known before flight. A program can sweep through many fin shapes and speeds far faster than tunnel testing can.

Each tunnel run costs time and money, and models must be built by hand. A checked program lets designers discard weak shapes early. The best few can then go to the tunnel for proof. Program reports like this one spread a single tool to every design office that needed fin data in the Saturn and missile era.
nasa-tm-19670009440-simultaneous-cloud-a:
B. A. Sparkman and G. T. Cherrix, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, wrote this preliminary report in February 1967. It presents cloud albedo measurements, measures of how much sunlight a surface reflects, taken at the same time from aircraft and from orbit. Matching the readings of different instruments was the point of the exercise.

Aircraft carried Sol-A-Meters and a medium resolution infrared radiometer, while the Nimbus II satellite measured with its own radiometer from space. The teams measured the reflectivity of clouds, desert, and ocean surfaces simultaneously. Instrument descriptions, the measurement method, and the data fill the short report. Good agreement was found among the coordinated measurements from all of the instruments, the abstract reports, which supported using the satellite readings with confidence.
nasa-tm-19670016998-stress-and-stability:
K. Schiffner wrote this study in German, published in April 1966 as a German aerospace research report. It investigates stress and stability in thin-wall conical shells under loads that are the same all around the axis. Cone-shaped shells appear often in rocket structures, where buckling under load can destroy a vehicle. The English translation was issued at Redstone Arsenal, Alabama, in January 1967.

Schiffner applies a nonlinear shell theory that allows large deformations. The first part describes the shell's unbuckled state under axial load and internal pressure, solving the governing equations by a refined difference method. An exact solution is also given for the simplified linear case. The second part computes buckling loads as an eigenvalue problem, solved step by step. Effects of shell proportions and of slight pre-deformation are discussed. Results agreed well with experiments, especially for axial load with high internal pressure.
nasa-tm-19670018236-galactic-x-rays-a-su:
Elihu Boldt, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this summary in May 1967. It was prepared for the 1968 Yearbook of Science and Technology, published by McGraw-Hill. The subject is galactic X-rays, high-energy radiation arriving from sources inside our own galaxy, a field then only five years old.

Rocket observations of solar X-rays had run for about twenty years, Boldt notes, but galactic X-ray astronomy began in 1962. A rocket team hunting lunar X-rays instead detected a strong source in Scorpius, named Sco X-1, outshining the quiet Sun at short wavelengths. Since then, rocket and balloon experiments had found at least thirty more discrete galactic sources. Balloons lift instruments above most of the atmosphere, and rockets go higher still. The summary reports the field's status just before the OSO-III satellite carried the first successful X-ray telescope into orbit in March 1967.
nasa-tm-19680018177-a-noncontacting-disp:
Eugene C. Naumann and Bruce Flagge of Langley Research Center present a displacement measuring technique that never touches the test object in this October 1966 conference paper. Vibration testing needs exact records of how parts move. Contact sensors can disturb light structures or fail under harsh shaking.

Flagge's part of the paper covers the instrumentation technique itself. Naumann's part covers its application to current vibration testing at Langley. The method measures displacement without contact, so the sensor adds no load to the structure. Engineers could thus record true motion during vibration tests. The paper was given at the Instrument Society of America conference in New York.
nasa-tm-19680026117-proton-and-ultra-vio:
C. A. Nicoletta of Goddard Space Flight Center reports irradiation tests on the RAE-A satellite's target sphere material in this August 1968 report. The material is zinc titanate over Lexan. Space radiation can darken such coatings and change how much sunlight they absorb.

One-inch samples were exposed to low energy protons, then to protons and ultraviolet light in sequence. A purpose-built system allowed optical reflectance measurements without removing the samples. Very little degradation appeared below a threshold proton flux. Above that threshold, solar absorptance rose rapidly, more so for the higher energy beam. Combined proton and ultraviolet exposure enhanced damage at first, then leveled off at higher fluxes.
nasa-tm-19700005739-stress-corrosion-cra:
James G. Williamson of the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this report on November 19, 1969. Its subject is stress corrosion cracking in one titanium alloy, Ti-6Al-4V. That kind of cracking can grow in a stressed metal when it touches certain fluids.

Williamson reports tests of the alloy in a range of fluids. The point was to learn which fluids attack the metal and how the damage grows. Builders of rockets and aircraft used such test results to judge where the alloy could serve safely and which fluids it had to avoid.
nasa-tm-19700020684-the-compressible-flo:
Robert E. Henry of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a 1970 heat transfer meeting in Monterey, California. It studies mixtures of two components in two phases as they rush through nozzles and orifices. Such mixtures mix gas and liquid in a single fast stream.

Henry builds a math model of the fastest discharge such a stream can reach. The model accounts for heat and push passing between the gas and liquid parts. It predicts the key pressure ratio and the flow rate from the starting conditions. Its results matched published air and water nozzle data well. He then extends the same model to flow through orifices.
nasa-tm-19700026456-convergence-accelera:
Speeding the convergence of the steepest descent method is the aim of this Houston internal note, number MSC-ED-R-67-52. It was issued by the Manned Spacecraft Center there. That method is a step-by-step way to find the best value of a problem, used here for flight path optimization work.

The note first defines the optimization problem and reviews earlier gradient methods as background. It then builds the gradient method twice, once under hard constraints and once under soft ones. For each form, a matching acceleration procedure follows, meant to reach the answer in fewer steps. An application with results tests the procedures, and appendices supply orbit parameters, the governing equations, and a worked example.
nasa-tm-19720002555-a-compilation-of-res:
A NASA preprint numbered X-752-71-351 compiles results on the behavior of phase locked loops; its author names are garbled in the scan. Phase locked loops are circuits that lock an oscillator onto an incoming signal. They sit inside radios, tracking receivers, and spacecraft communications gear.

The volume sums up the state of the art for engineers who design with these loops. A terminology section fixes working definitions, and an index organizes the compiled results. Results are grouped by their describing equations and by the jobs loops do: acquisition, tracking, and detection. Each result is presented with its assumptions and source references. An example problem works the methods end to end, and a closing section points to future work.
nasa-tm-19720004463-graphic-displays-for:
Daniel L Whipple of the Lewis Research Center described a display system for large test facilities in November 1971, as NASA TM X-67968. Wind tunnel crews once waited for printed results after each run. Whipple's system put live data on screens in the control room. It joined new software with display hardware on a shared computer. Engineers could watch a test unfold and react at once.

Users could call up numbers or graphs as they wished. Hard copy printouts were available from the same screens. Helper programs allowed editing of graphics while the test ran. They also handled program control, data changes, and later microfilm output. The setup brought interactive computing into daily tunnel work.
nasa-tm-19720019561-application-of-an-on:
W. N. Stewart and colleagues wrote this NASA preprint, numbered X-715-72-226, on putting a real computer aboard the OAO C spacecraft. OAO was the Orbiting Astronomical Observatory series, and OAO C was its fourth spacecraft. The machine they describe, called OBP 1, is a stored-program computer built for spacecraft use.

The abstract describes a medium-scale machine that works in parallel and holds more than sixteen thousand words of memory, running on modest power. Aboard OAO C its jobs would include storing commands, monitoring the spacecraft, and reporting malfunctions. It would also compress data, summarize status, and possibly take emergency corrective action in some abnormal situations. The report covers the computer's history, its interfaces with the spacecraft, and its memory, processor, and input-output units in detail.
nomads-of-the-north-a-story-of-romance-a:
James Oliver Curwood called Nomads of the North a story of romance and adventure under the open stars. It opens in late March, at the dying out of the Eagle Moon. Neewa, a black bear cub, gets his first real look at the world that month.

His mother Noozak is an old bear, full of rheumatics and a wish to sleep late. She slept four months that winter, not the usual three, in a cavern on a high, barren ridge. Neewa was born while she slept soundly. From the den he looks down on a valley between Jackson's Knee and the Shamattawa River, as early spring works its change.
occasional-papers-selected-from-the-guar:
Richard William Church wrote essays for three major papers. They appeared in the Guardian, the Times, and the Saturday Review. The pieces date from 1846 to 1890. Volume two was printed in London in 1897. Church had served as Dean of Saint Paul's.

The contents focus on church and state in Victorian England. Essays treat Gladstone, court judgments, and disendowment of the church. Other pieces review books by Renan and other writers. Church writes as a careful churchman and critic. The volume preserves informed debate from a long career. Later pieces treat new courts and church reform plans in detail.
outlines-of-lessons-in-botany-part-i-fro: Jane H. Newell's Outlines of Lessons in Botany is a teaching manual from 1888. Part One runs From Seed to Leaf. Teachers, or mothers studying with their children, are its audience. The hosted sample shows the title page and contents only. The course opens with plants and their uses. Seedlings raised in the schoolroom follow, then roots and root-hairs. Buds and branches close the part. No lesson text appears.
over-the-top-by-an-american-soldier-who-:
Arthur Guy Empey was an American who enlisted in the British army. He served as a machine gunner in France. Over the Top came out of the trenches. By its twenty-sixth impression it was America's most famous soldier's book of the war. It comes together with Tommy's Dictionary of the Trenches, his glossary of the soldiers' slang.

His foreword argues the Allied cause from sixteen years of roughing it around the world, before the mast and in the trenches. The average American, he says, mistakes the Englishman for a distant, humorless man; Tommy Atkins proved himself the best of mates, bubbling with humor, willing to sacrifice everything but honor. Empey's book sold the British Tommy to America in Tommy's own voice.
raphael-a-collection-of-fifteen-pictures: Raphael, a collection of fifteen pictures and a portrait of the painter, edited by Estelle M. Hurll in the Masterpieces of Art series, was published at Boston and New York by Houghton Mifflin Company with an 1899 copyright. The pages shown give the contents. Raphael's self-portrait serves as frontispiece. It comes from a photograph by Fratelli Alinari. Sections on his character as an artist follow. Books of reference come next. A historical directory of the pictures appears. Collateral reading, an outline of his life, and his contemporaries close the list.
sanders-union-fourth-reader-embracing-a-:
Charles W. Sanders, A.M., wrote Sanders' Union Fourth Reader, embracing a full exposition of the principles of rhetorical reading, with many exercises for practice in prose and poetry. The exercises are varied in style and carefully fitted to teaching in schools of every grade. In the preface Sanders explains the design of the Fourth Reader. It is made to pass the pupil from the easier ground of the Third to the harder course of the Union Fifth Reader. That Reader is next higher in the series. The book is carefully graded to that middle position.

In one sense, Sanders argues, the Fourth Reader is the most important in the set. The great mass of pupils in common schools are drawn away from school pursuits long before the proper time for a more advanced course. That fact weighed fully in preparing the pages.
snowflakes-and-sunbeams-or-the-young-fur: R. M. Ballantyne wrote The Young Fur-Traders, and the contents open in the middle of an Arctic winter in the wilds of North America. Heads bring in the old fur-trader, who tries to fix his son's flint and finds the task hard, then a counting-room scene. A wolf-hunt on the prairies follows, where Charley stuns his father and breaks in the new horse. Peter Mactavish turns amateur doctor, and Charley airs his views to Kate before the spring brigade sets out.
studies-in-the-psychology-of-sex-volume-:
Volume V of Havelock Ellis's Studies in the Psychology of Sex, dated 1927, holds Erotic Symbolism, The Mechanism of Detumescence, and The Psychic State in Pregnancy. Ellis calls these the terminal phenomena of the sexual process, treated before the final volume turns to morals and social hygiene.

Under erotic symbolism Ellis places nearly all the stray forms of the sexual instinct. In each, he argues, some object or act has gained a dynamic power over the mind and body: clear in shoe fetishism, dimmer in exhibitionism. Calling them sexual equivalents only labels them; symbolism, he claims, gives the key that makes them intelligible, whether their roots are inborn, acquired, or both.
ten-reasons-proposed-to-his-adversaries-:
Edmund Campion, a priest of the Society of Jesus, wrote Ten Reasons, his Decem Rationes, as a challenge to foes of the Catholic faith at the English universities. An opening essay in this printing traces the work's long life and high praise.

The essay notes forty-seven printings across Europe and a verdict by Mark Anthony Muret that it was written by the finger of God. It calls the work Campion's last free word on his brief English mission. He had checked the tide of the new faith when the old church seemed down for good. Readers get a famed piece of Elizabethan religious debate, framed by its martyr's fate.
the-abolition-of-slavery-the-right-of-th:
William Lloyd Garrison and others stand behind The Abolition of Slavery. Its full title claims the right of the government under the war power. The pieces argue that the federal war power can end slavery. A part on freedom under the war power opens the book.

That part quotes John Quincy Adams at length. Adams spoke in the House on April 14 and 15, 1842. The topic was war with Great Britain and Mexico. Adams grants that Congress may not meddle with slavery in the states. That holds while slave states keep to their own bounds. But the case changes once the topic is forced on the House. It changes once a member is censured unheard. Readers get a core legal case for wartime freedom. It was built from speeches made years before the Civil War.
the-authoritative-life-of-general-willia:
G. S. Railton, described as first commissioner to General Booth, wrote an authorised life of William Booth, founder of the Salvation Army. Booth was born on April 10, 1829, and died on August 20, 1912, the year this life was copyrighted. A preface by General Bramwell Booth opens the volume.

Twenty-eight chapters trace Booth from childhood and poverty through youth, lay work, and early ministry. Later chapters follow work in East London, the making of an army, and growth in America, Australasia, India, South Africa, and Japan. Final sections cover social work, finance, old age, tributes, organisation, and Booth as a writer.
the-circus-boys-on-the-flying-rings-or-m:
Edgar B. P. Darlington opens this boys' circus tale, subtitled Making the Start in the Sawdust Life, with two boys before a circus billboard. Teddy boasts that he can do what the pictured performer is doing in the air. Phil, his friend, laughs the claim down and corrects his terms.

That is no cartwheel, Phil tells him, but a double somersault, and a real stunt at that. The contents then follow Phil's path: he hears his dismissal, makes his start in the world, and proves his mettle when the circus comes to town. He makes friends with the elephants, enters the sawdust arena, and wins his first call and a thrilling rescue. Setbacks follow, including being left behind and a startling discovery. Darlington gives young readers a backstage path into circus work, from first longing to a solved mystery.
the-collected-works-of-ambrose-bierce-vo: Volume VIII of Ambrose Bierce's collected works gathers his Negligible Tales, On with the Dance, and his Epigrams, shown here in a Gordian Press reprint of 1966. The title page notes that the volume was originally published in 1911. Only the front matter is present here, including the publisher's imprint and Library of Congress card number.A title page and a contents list are all that stand here.
the-continental-monthly-vol-iii-issue-vi:
June 1863 brings the sixth number of volume III of The Continental Monthly, devoted to literature and national policy. Its lead piece is the second part of The Value of the Union. Having surveyed the Union's worth and growth in the first part, the writer now turns to face the pro-slavery rebellion and its drift.

The argument runs through sacred history: a kind Providence, the essay says, has always pushed mankind toward a higher, more united, and happier life, against the drag of selfishness and ignorance. Ages of political upheaval and such religious light as men could take in raised Europe to its state of two and a half centuries ago. There the seeds of religious and political liberty sprouted and crossed to the new world, where they grew into the republic.
the-divine-right-of-church-government-wh: The Divine Right of Church Government argues that rule by preaching and ruling elders alone can claim God's warrant from Scripture. The title page credits sundry ministers of Christ in London. It notes a new, corrected edition printed in New York in 1844. An added part draws on strong writers about church rule. Only the title pages are present here. Their lines cover who may preach, who may join a church, and the people's right to choose pastors.
the-golden-treasury-of-the-best-songs-an: Francis Turner Palgrave selected The Golden Treasury of the Best Songs and Lyrical Pieces in the English Language. Collins' Clear-Type Press printed it in London and Glasgow. Pictures are by A. Pearse. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and Palgrave's dedication to Alfred Tennyson, Poet Laureate. In it he says the book grew under Tennyson's advice. He had hoped to dedicate it to Henry Hallam, who died before it was done. He calls it a true national anthology of three centuries.
the-great-lone-land-a-narrative-of-trave:
Colonel W. F. Butler wrote The Great Lone Land. It is a narrative of travel and adventure in the North-West of America. Sampson Low, Marston and Company printed it in London.
